sweeps.topic: Discrete behavior tokenization from continuous demonstrations for a 50 Hz body lane (VQ-BeT / BeT / ACT / FAST / quadruped motion codebooks) and decodability of codes by a Go2 tracking policy

findings.claim: VQ-BeT tokenizes actions with a residual VQ of only Nq=2 layers and 8-16 codes per layer (64-256 combinations) plus a continuous offset head; enlarging the codebook up to 65,536 combinations gave minimal change, while removing residual VQ or the offset head hurts significantly. It beats Diffusion Policy on 7 environments at 15 ms/step vs ~100 ms.
findings.source_title: Behavior Generation with Latent Actions (VQ-BeT), ICML 2024 Spotlight
findings.numbers: Nq=2; codebook 8-16/layer; latent 512-D (256 BlockPush); transformer 6L/6H/120-D; PushT IoU 0.78 vs 0.74 DP; Kitchen 3.66 vs 3.44; Ant 3.22 vs 2.90; real robot 47/50 and 19/30 vs DP 45/50 and 11/30 (+73% long-horizon); 15.1 ms vs 100.5 ms per step; robot CPU 207 ms vs 5,244 ms; codebook ablation 100->1,024->4,096->65,536 combos: Ant 3.22->3.01->3.11, Kitchen 3.66->3.75->3.7; LeRobot defaults vqvae_n_embed 16, embedding 256, action_chunk_size 5, n_action_pred_token 3, 20k VQ steps, offset_loss_weight 10000, temperature 0.1; official code MIT, paper CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Sets the codebook size class and structure (small RVQ + offset) for Parcel's body lane; code is MIT/Apache via LeRobot.

findings.claim: FAST shows naive per-frame binning fails at 20-50 Hz because marginal information per frame approaches zero (the model copies the first action), and compresses a 1 s, 50 Hz, 14-D chunk from 700 to 53 tokens with DCT+BPE; FAST+ is a universal tokenizer over 1M chunks at 5-50 Hz, but autoregressive decode costs ~750 ms per chunk.
findings.source_title: FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models
findings.numbers: DCT scale gamma=10; BPE vocab 1024; 1 s chunks; tokens/chunk naive->FAST: BridgeV2 5 Hz 35->20 (1.75x), DROID 15 Hz 105->29 (3.6x), bussing 20 Hz 140->28 (5.0x), T-shirt 50 Hz 14-D 700->53 (13.2x); FAST+ 1M chunks, 5-50 Hz, 7-40-D; 5x fewer GPU-hours than pi0; ~750 ms decode per chunk (30-60 tokens) vs ~100 ms diffusion; CC BY 4.0; HF AutoProcessor
findings.relevance: Hard evidence against emitting one body token per 50 Hz frame; also shows FAST's ~50 tok/s and 750 ms decode are too dense/slow for a 12.5 Hz shared speech clock.

findings.claim: QUART-Online VQ-encodes chunks of a 12-D quadruped command vector (512 codes x 2 residual layers) so a 5 Hz MLLM emitting 10-step chunks synchronizes with a 50 Hz controller (f_l = l_ac x f_m), raising task success by ~65% with chunk reconstruction MAE 0.012 / PSNR 32.1.
findings.source_title: QUART-Online: Latency-Free Large Multimodal Language Model for Quadruped Robot Learning
findings.numbers: codebook 512 codes/layer, Nq=2, D=512; chunk lengths 1/5/10; 12-D commands (11 + terminate); 10 x 5 Hz = 50 Hz; unseen-visual avg 0.37->0.68, unseen-language 0.52->0.79; Distinguish 0.90/0.99, Go-to 0.89/1.00, Go-avoid 0.58/0.80; MAE 0.012, AKI 0.0008, PSNR 32.11, UQI 0.9999; 2 Hz -> 50 Hz; Isaac Gym; code github.com/yuan48/QUART-Online
findings.relevance: The only quadruped precedent for VQ chunk tokens driving a 50 Hz controller; its command-level payload is the abstraction Parcel's tracker consumes.

findings.claim: On a real Unitree Go2, a motion latent produced at 2 Hz and executed by a single universal 50 Hz PPO tracker runs end-to-end in under 500 ms on a Jetson Orin (QuadFM/Gen2Control); the latent is a continuous VAE code, not a discrete codebook.
findings.source_title: QuadFM: a foundational text-driven quadruped motion dataset + Gen2Control RL
findings.numbers: 11,784 clips, 20.27 h, 3.64M frames @50 Hz, 35,352 texts; generator 2 Hz (MotionGPT3-style VAE+diffusion), tracker MLP 2048-1024-512-256 @50 Hz; Go2 X + Orin <500 ms; 20,000 PPO iterations; MJPE 0.0712 rad, MBPE 0.0744 m; human eval 7.98/9 text alignment; CC BY 4.0; dataset not yet released
findings.relevance: Proves the latent->tracker route on Parcel's exact hardware and latency budget; quantizing that latent is the missing (buildable) step.

findings.claim: Uni-Mo's tracking policies on a real Unitree Go2 achieve 96.7% success over 392 randomly sampled expressive motions (5 trials each) and 97.6% in sim over 7,488 motions, with the 19-D, 50 Hz Quad-Imaginarium dataset released under CC BY 4.0.
findings.source_title: Unleashing Infinite Motion: Scaling Expressive Quadrupedal Motion via Generative Video Priors (Uni-Mo)
findings.numbers: 7,488 motions, 18.5 h; 19-D state (root pos 3 + quat 4 + 12 joints) @50 Hz; clips 5-15 s mean 8.9 s; retention 68.1% (CLIP>=0.85 97.0%, geometric 70.2%); sim 97.6%; real 96.7% over 392 x 5; MBPE 40.6 mm, MRPE 3.8 cm, MROE 2.7 deg, MPJPE 3.4 deg; CC BY 4.0; github GaoLii/Quad-Imaginarium
findings.relevance: The largest license-clean Go2-native expressive clip corpus to fit a body tokenizer on, and the acceptance-bar numbers for tracking reconstructed codes.

findings.claim: MotionGlot tokenizes quadruped (Spot) motion with a per-embodiment VQ-VAE of 128 codes x 512-D at 4 poses per token (12.5 tokens/s at 50 Hz) and a GPT-2-small generates text-conditioned locomotion from a 2.5 h dataset.
findings.source_title: MotionGlot: A Multi-Embodied Motion Generation Model
findings.numbers: codebook R^{128x512}; l=4; QUAD-LOCO >1,000 trajectories / 2.5 h on Spot, ~48,000 pairs after augmentation; R-precision@1/2/3 0.18/0.35/0.48; diversity 3.74; BLEU@4 36.5; +31.2% avg over baselines; 8x A5000, ~20k steps; CC BY 4.0; code on GitHub, dataset 'to be released soon'
findings.relevance: A 128-code, 4-frames-per-token quadruped vocabulary suffices for language-conditioned generation - the size class Parcel should start at.

findings.claim: Tencent's VQ-PMC uses a discrete latent of K=256 codes x 32-D, queried at 50 Hz over a 500 Hz PD loop, trained on ~39 min of Labrador mocap, and drives a real quadruped (MAX) through a three-level hierarchy that beat a human-operated robot 2:0 at chase-tag.
findings.source_title: Lifelike Agility and Play in Quadrupedal Robots using RL and Generative Pre-trained Models (VQ-PMC)
findings.numbers: K=256, D=32, beta=0.25; ~30 min + 9 min mocap at 120 fps; PMC 50 Hz, PD 500 Hz; primitive level 2 days on 2x V100, environmental 4 days on 4x V100, strategic 40 h; code + mocap released (research-only)
findings.relevance: Earliest real-quadruped proof that a 256-entry discrete latent at 50 Hz decodes to lifelike dog motion via a learned low-level controller.

findings.claim: Walk Like Dogs builds a Go2 pipeline from 13,076 dog pose samples: kino-dynamic retargeting (MJPC), an 18-D hyperspherical VAE whose modes Pace/Trot/Gallop emerge automatically, and a 50 Hz PPO tracker (IsaacLab, 4,096 envs) with 0.11 m base-velocity RMSE; the latent is continuous.
findings.source_title: Walk Like Dogs: Learning Steerable Imitation Controllers for Legged Robots from Unlabeled Motion Data
findings.numbers: 13,076 samples + mirrors; IK scales alpha_z 0.81, fwd 0.6, side 0.6; MJPC iLQG T=2.0 s dt 0.01 s; vMF latent 18-D; MoE decoder 6 experts; PPO batch 4,096, lr 5e-4; 50 Hz; velocity RMSE 0.11 m; gait switch at 1.8/1.2/0.7 m/s; real Go2 qualitative
findings.relevance: Go2-native reference pipeline whose emergent gait modes are the natural targets a VQ layer would snap to.

findings.claim: ACT commits to action chunks of k=100 at 50 Hz (2 s) with an 80M-param CVAE-transformer; chunk-size ablation goes from 1% success at k=1 to 44% at k=100, and inference takes ~10 ms.
findings.source_title: Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware (ACT)
findings.numbers: k=100; 50 Hz; ~80M params (4 enc/7 dec, 512-D, 8 heads); CVAE beta=10; 50 demos/task (~10 min); episodes 400-700 steps; k=1 1%, k=10 ~15%, k=100 44%, k=200-400 slight decline; real tasks 86/93/84/92%; inference ~0.01 s; temporal ensemble w_i=exp(-m*i)
findings.relevance: Evidence that a 50 Hz policy should emit whole chunks and blend them (temporal ensembling), which is how 12.5 Hz body tokens get interpolated to 50 Hz.

findings.claim: BeT (the VQ-BeT ancestor) discretizes actions with k-means (k=24-64 per environment) plus a continuous residual offset, reconstructing a = A[a] + <a>; VQ-BeT later notes k-means does not scale to high-dimensional or temporally extended actions.
findings.source_title: Behavior Transformers: Cloning k modes with one stone
findings.numbers: k: Point-mass 2/3, CARLA 32, Block-push 24, Kitchen 64; context 2/10/5/10; ~1e4-1e6 params; CARLA 0.98; Block-push 2 blocks 0.71 vs ~0; Kitchen entropy 2.47 vs 2.96 demos; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Origin of the discrete-mode + continuous-residual pattern; explains why a chunked RVQ is preferred over per-step k-means.

findings.claim: B-spline tokenizers give a fixed small token count per chunk without tokenizer training: BEAST uses 5-10 control points per 1 s chunk (4-8x fewer than binning, MSE 0.0004 vs 0.0215, 19 ms/chunk parallel decode), and OmniSAT adds an 8-layer RVQ (codebooks 256/256/64) for 6.8x compression, beating FAST (3.7x) and BEAST (4.6x) on real tasks.
findings.source_title: OmniSAT: Compact Action Token, Faster Autoregression (with BEAST, arXiv 2506.06072v2)
findings.numbers: BEAST: N=5-10 tokens per 1 s, 256 bins, 617 Hz throughput, CALVIN 99.8%, LIBERO-LONG 86.4% vs pi0-FAST 60.2%, real 76.57%, BEAST-ACT 70% vs 49%, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. OmniSAT: Tc=8, degree 4, RVQ L=8, codebooks 256/256/64, BPE 2048, 30 frames @30 Hz, compression 6.8x/8.1x, DROID MAE 9.4e-4 vs BEAST 8.0e-2, LIBERO 93.4%, real 73/63/48% vs 63/45/23%, CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Training-free fallback (BEAST) if a learned codebook collapses on a small dog-clip library, and a smooth-basis + small-RVQ recipe (OmniSAT) for body-pose chunks.

findings.claim: Recent RVQ action tokenizers keep converging on 4 frames per token and 256-2048 codes per level with data at scale: X-Tokenizer (4 levels x 2048, r=4, 2.4M trajectories) trades +17% reconstruction error vs FAST for +10 points real success; VQ-VLA (256 codes/layer, chunk 5) triples OpenVLA inference rate to 11.84 Hz and shows tokenizer quality scales with 100x sim data.
findings.source_title: X-Tokenizer: A Multimodal Action Tokenizer for VLA Pretraining (with VQ-VLA, ICCV 2025, arXiv 2507.01016)
findings.numbers: X-Tokenizer: Q=4, V=2048, r=4 (64 frames -> 16 slots), D=26, 2.4M trajectories / 2.0B frames, 17 arm families, l1 0.01693 vs FAST 0.01446, real 85.9% vs 75.7%, RoboTwin 69.25% vs 61.0%, CC BY 4.0. VQ-VLA: 256 codes/layer, K=5, LIBERO-90 80.98% vs 73.53%, real 23%->46.25%, 11.84 Hz vs 4.16 Hz, one A100 one week, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
findings.relevance: Supports pretraining Parcel's body tokenizer on sim rollouts and training the first RVQ level for semantics (masked action modeling) so tokens carry behavior meaning for the language model.

findings.claim: Discrete motion tokens decoded by 50 Hz trackers are now standard on Unitree humanoids: Heracles uses FSQ tokens with a 25 Hz generative middleware and 50 Hz policy on a G1 (90.6% completion); Humanoid-LLA uses a unified VQ motion vocabulary executed by a CVAE student policy (87.6% sim success, MPJPE 56 mm) on G1/Booster T1.
findings.source_title: Heracles: Bridging Precise Tracking and Generative Synthesis for General Humanoid Control (with Humanoid-LLA, arXiv 2511.22963v2)
findings.numbers: Heracles: iFSQ levels L=2^K+1; 38-D/35-D state; G1 29 DoF; 50 Hz policy, 200 Hz physics, 25 Hz middleware; 16,384 envs on one A100; completion 90.6% vs 84.8%; fall-recovery 90.0% vs 44.0%. Humanoid-LLA: 26,846 AMASS sequences; success 87.6%; MPJPE 56.43 mm; FID 2.626; R-precision 0.447; CC BY 4.0; code 'coming soon'
findings.relevance: Same hardware family as the Go2; shows the LLM-emits-motion-tokens -> tracker executes pattern transfers to real Unitree platforms.

findings.claim: A 50 Hz tracking stack for a quadruped behavior foundation model runs on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB (ABot-C0: 200 Hz motor loop, 50 Hz decision/tracking, flow policy with 5 ODE steps), and intensity/style can be a runtime scalar rather than extra codes (DFM tempo 0.5-1.5x on aibo; AMOR weight conditioning).
findings.source_title: Behavior Foundations for Quadruped Robots: ABot-C0 Technical Report (with DFM arXiv 2502.10980 and AMOR arXiv 2505.23708)
findings.numbers: ABot-C0: 16,074 trajectories / 22.43 h; 32-D VAE latent; seen 92.74% / unseen 88.54%; MPJPE 12.38/14.79 mm; AGX Orin 64 GB; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. DFM: c=8 Fourier channels (24-D), 34 dances x 5 tempos = 170 clips x 6 s, 100 Hz, MAE 0.094 vs 0.132 rad. AMOR: 7 reward terms, 300k iters ~5 days on one RTX 4090, tuning 1 day vs 5-day retrain, smoothness weight reduces sim-to-real gap
findings.relevance: Confirms Orin headroom for the body-side models and gives two precedents for expressing 'how much' (intensity) outside the codebook.

design_implications: Body-lane token rate: one token per 80 ms (4 frames at 50 Hz = 12.5 tok/s), aligned one-to-one with Mimi/Moshi speech frames; never per-frame at 50 Hz (FAST shows per-frame binning collapses; MotionGlot/X-Tokenizer/MoReFlow/Beyond-MoCap all use 4 frames per token).

Codebook: residual VQ with Nq=2, 16-64 codes per layer for a 30-100 clip dog library (VQ-BeT: 8-16 sufficed and 65,536 combos did not help; quadruped codebooks in the wild are 128-512), primary code = behavior mode (chuckle, look-back, play-bow, gait), secondary = variation, plus a continuous offset head; put intensity in a scalar (DFM tempo 0.5-1.5x / AMOR-style tracker weights) rather than more codes; use EMA/FSQ to avoid dead codes.

Token payload is a chunk of command-level or reference-pose state (QUART-Online 12-D command x 10 steps; Uni-Mo 19-D root+quat+12 joints), decoded by ONE universal 50 Hz PPO tracker trained on the whole clip library; only the tracker touches the robot, so any sampled token is physically executable.

Go2 decodability is a build task with public parts: quantize a QuadFM/Walk-Like-Dogs-style Go2 latent, fit the RVQ (LeRobot vqbet defaults, 20k steps), retrain the tracker overnight (4,096 envs on one RTX-class GPU), and accept at sim success >=95% / MPJPE <= ~4 deg on token-reconstructed references (Uni-Mo bar); latency budget <500 ms end-to-end is already demonstrated on Go2 + Orin.

Data/licences: fit on Quad-Imaginarium (7,488 Go2 motions, CC BY 4.0) + Kine2Go (800 Go2 trajectories, CC BY 4.0) + Parcel's authored expressive clips; Tencent Labrador mocap is research-only; QuadFM/DogML not yet usable; ABot-C0 is CC BY-NC-ND. Tokenizer code: VQ-BeT (MIT), LeRobot vqbet (Apache-2.0), RDT2 RVQActionTokenizer (Apache-2.0); avoid VQ-VLA/BEAST code (CC BY-NC-SA) for product use.
Do not use FAST for the shared-clock body lane (~53 tok/s at 50 Hz 14-D and ~750 ms autoregressive decode per 1 s chunk); keep FAST/FAST+ only if the body lane is moved to a separate slow VLA.

Learning 'chuckle if funny' / 'look back when lost' reduces to shifting the probability of a few primary codes at the right conversational moment (a 1-2 s motif is 12-25 tokens); this keeps the reward-learning problem in the small-discrete-action regime where ~4 preference queries suffice (LGPL) and bandits/preference RL from the first sweep apply.

results.claim: VQ-BeT tokenizes actions with a residual VQ of only Nq=2 layers and 8-16 codes per layer (64-256 combinations) plus a continuous offset head; enlarging the codebook up to 65,536 combinations gave minimal change, while removing residual VQ or the offset head hurts significantly. It beats Diffusion Policy on 7 environments at 15 ms/step vs ~100 ms.
results.evidence_quote: "In all of our experiments, it was sufficient to use Nq:=2 VQ-residual layers" ... "not using a residual VQ layer has a significant negative impact, which we believe is because of the lack of expressivity from a single VQ-layer." ... "we found that the offset prediction is quite important for VQ-BeT" ... Table 3 (Kitchen): VQ-BeT single step 15.1ms; DiffusionPolicy-C 100.5ms; DiffusionPolicy-T 98.6ms ... Table 12: Kitchen (Conditional) codebook 16 -> 256 combinations 3.78; codebook 256 -> 65536 combinations 3.61; Ant 100 combos 3.22 vs 1024 combos 3.01/3.11; Kitchen 256 combos 3.66 vs 4096 combos 3.75/3.7 ... Abstract: "Across seven environments including simulated manipulation, autonomous driving, and robotics, VQ-BeT improves on state-of-the-art models" ... BUT: "In BlockPush environment, VQ-BeT is outperformed by DiffusionPolicy-T, while in Image Kitchen it is outperformed by DiffusionPolicy-C." (Table 2: BlockPush VQ-BeT 1.79 vs DP-T 1.93; Image Kitchen VQ-BeT 2.98 vs DP-C 3.11).
results.correction: Structure, ablations and timing hold: Nq=2 residual VQ layers, codebooks of 10-16 codes/layer in the main configs (100-256 combinations; the conditional Ant run uses 48/layer = 2,304), plus an observation-conditioned offset head; removing residual VQ or the offset head is stated (qualitatively, no numbers in prose) to hurt significantly; growing to 4,096 combos changed Ant 3.22->3.01/3.11 and Kitchen 3.66->3.75/3.7, and 65,536 combos (Kitchen conditional) went 3.78->3.61, i.e. no gain. Inference is 15.1 ms vs 100.5 ms (DP-C) / 98.6 ms (DP-T) per step on GPU in Kitchen (Table 3); on the real-robot table it is 18.06 vs 573.49 ms GPU and 207.25 vs 5,243.82 ms CPU. However, VQ-BeT does NOT beat Diffusion Policy on all seven environments: the paper explicitly says DP-T wins BlockPush (1.93 vs 1.79) and DP-C wins Image Kitchen (3.11 vs 2.98) in the unconditional setting; VQ-BeT wins the other 5 of 7 (PushT 0.78 vs 0.74, Image PushT 0.68 vs 0.66, Kitchen 3.66 vs 3.44, Ant 3.22 vs 2.90/3.12, UR3 BlockPush 1.84 vs 1.83). Restate as: 'evaluated across seven environments, matching or exceeding SOTA overall, beating DP on 5/7 unconditional tasks.' The '8-16 codes per layer' should be '10-16 (up to 48) codes per layer'. The MIT code-license claim is not verifiable from the paper (paper itself is CC BY 4.0).

Two precision notes: (1) the 'copies the first action' observation comes from the synthetic time-series experiment in Fig. 3 (sampling rates 25-800 steps), while the 20 Hz bussing and 50 Hz T-shirt robot tasks are reported as naive-tokenization policies being 'unable to make progress'; (2) the 5-50 Hz / 7-40-D range for FAST+ is inferred from the appendix dataset-mix table (Table III), not stated as a single sentence in prose. The 750 ms figure is measured on an NVIDIA 4090.

results.evidence_quote: "The learnable codebook B ∈ R^{Nq×K×D} consists of Nq layers of codes ... The input vector of each layer is the residual from the previous quantization step." ... "512 dimensions and 512 quantizers (Nq=2)" ... "we treat the sequence of N consecutive action commands at time T as a set of input action commands Ac={ai}i=T..T+N ∈ R^{N×12}" ... "11-dimensional high-level commands as well as a terminate signal, i.e., [vx,vy,ωz,θ1,θ2,θ3,f,hz,ϕ,sy,hzf,e]" ... "three different action chunk lengths (1, 5, and 10)" ... "fl = lac × fm" ... Table II: QUART 2HZ; QUART-Online-1 5HZ; QUART-Online-10 50HZ ... "achieving real-time inference at 50Hz in sync with the underlying controller frequency" ... "significantly boosting the success rate across various tasks by 65%" ... Reconstruction (N=10): "MAE(↓) 0.012, AKI(↓) 0.0008, PSNR(↑) 32.11, UQI(↑) 0.9999" ... "NVIDIA's Isaac Gym".
results.correction: Claim holds. Notes: the paper's wording is '512 dimensions and 512 quantizers (Nq=2)' (K=512 codes, D=512, two residual layers); the 5 Hz MLLM rate is given by the Table II row 'QUART-Online-1 | 5HZ' (chunk length 1) and the formula f_l = l_ac × f_m, so 10 × 5 Hz = 50 Hz for QUART-Online-10; the baseline QUART runs at 2 Hz. The paper links only the project page https://quart-online.github.io — the GitHub URL github.com/yuan48/QUART-Online in the numbers field does not appear in the paper and is unverified.

results.claim: On a real Unitree Go2, a motion latent produced at 2 Hz and executed by a single universal 50 Hz PPO tracker runs end-to-end in under 500 ms on a Jetson Orin (QuadFM/Gen2Control); the latent is a continuous VAE code, not a discrete codebook.
results.evidence_quote: "The motion generator runs at 2Hz to produce motion commands, while the generic locomotion controller executes them at 50Hz for stable tracking." ... "Our end-to-end real-robot deployment runs on a Unitree GO2 X quadruped, where both the motion generator and the low-level controller are deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin" ... "achieving real-time motion synthesis (<500 ms latency)" / "the overall latency from speech input to motion execution is approximately 0.5s." ... "A motion VAE encodes a motion clip m_{1:M} into a latent z = E(m_{1:M})" (diffusion model pθ(z|c,st); initialized from MotionGPT3; no VQ/codebook/discrete-token mention) ... BUT the tracker consumes the DECODED motion, not the latent: "decode a reference motion: m̂₁:ₘ = D(z)" and "Given the current proprioception and a short future window of the reference motion, the tracking policy outputs low-level actions: u_k = π_φ(s_k, τ^(i))" ... tracker: "4-layer MLPs with hidden dimensions 2048, 1024, 512, and 256", "train πϕ with PPO", "20,000 iterations", "a general motion tracking policy that executes generated motions robustly" ... "The dataset will be released at https://github.com/GaoLii/QuadFM" ... License: CC BY 4.0.
results.correction: Hardware, rates, latency and 'continuous VAE latent, no codebook' all check out (Unitree GO2 X, Jetson Orin running both generator and controller, 2 Hz generator, 50 Hz PPO MLP tracker, <500 ms / ~0.5 s speech-to-motion). The mischaracterization is the interface: the tracker does not execute the latent. The generator samples a continuous latent z via diffusion, DECODES it with the VAE decoder into a reference motion m̂ = D(z) (kinematic joint/body trajectory), and the tracking policy takes proprioception plus a short future window of that decoded reference motion. So the paper proves a 'text -> latent -> decoded reference trajectory -> universal tracker' route on Go2/Orin, not a 'latent -> tracker' route; quantizing the latent would still require the VAE decoder in the loop before the tracker. Also: the paper never explicitly calls the latent 'continuous'; that is inferred from the VAE+diffusion (MotionGPT3-style) design and the absence of any VQ/codebook.

sweeps.topic: Templates for adding a non-speech token stream (act OUT) and world-state conditioning (world IN) to Moshi: Moshi-Face, MoshiVis, and other 2025-2026 Moshi/Mimi-family stream extensions

findings.claim: Moshi-Face adds facial motion as N=8 parallel discrete tokens per 12.5 Hz frame (codebook K=256, dim 128), read as input streams for both speakers (2N in) and generated for the system (N out) by a non-autoregressive 'Face Transformer' side head conditioned on the Temporal Transformer hidden state plus the frame's text and audio token embeddings — not as extra Depth-Transformer codebooks.
findings.source_title: Integrating Facial Generation into Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems (Moshi-Face), Jiang, Ohashi, Higashinaka, Nagoya Univ., Interspeech 2026
findings.numbers: 12.5 Hz face tokens (25 fps in, downsample r=2); N=8 tokens/frame; K=256, C=128 (MVE 9.90e-3, LVE 11.77e-3); face streams delayed 1 step vs text like audio; loss L_text+L_audio+lambda*L_face, lambda=1; Eq.2: e_All = h_{i+1} + e_text + sum of 8 audio embeddings; learnable positional embedding per output position; N per-component linear heads; Face Transformer size NOT reported.
findings.relevance: The most direct published recipe for Parcel's body/act stream: small parallel token set on Moshi's clock, fed back as input, emitted by one extra non-AR pass per frame. The user's face stream is a worked example of a world-state input stream on the same clock.

findings.claim: Moshi-Face was trained on ~180 h (~3,400 dialogues) of Seamless Interaction data with a two-step schedule (frozen Moshi + head, then joint full fine-tune); on LLM-judge dialogue metrics it matches original Moshi, but the 180 h fine-tune halves UTMOS speech naturalness (an effect the audio-only Moshi-ft control shares), and the frozen-backbone ablation gives chance-level lip sync — joint fine-tuning was 'essential'.
findings.source_title: Integrating Facial Generation into Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems (Moshi-Face) — Table 2 and Section 3
findings.numbers: Step 1: lr 5e-4, 500 steps, batch 32; Step 2: lr 2e-6/4e-6/1e-5 (Temporal/Depth/Face), 1,200 steps, batch 16; base kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16. Table 2: Moshi UTMOS 3.08, Coh 3.76, Nat 3.73, Rel 4.26, Ove 3.85; Moshi-ft 1.69/3.59/4.28/3.95/3.55; Moshi-Face 1.75/3.79/4.52/4.24/3.76; LSE-D teacher-forced 8.76 (upper bound 8.53, random 11.7), free-run 11.0; w/o full FT: LSE-D 11.8, UTMOS 2.42, Ove 3.23; w/o Step-1 pretrain: LSE-D 9.53. No latency, GPU, or wall-clock reported. No code/weights released.
findings.relevance: Sets Parcel's expectations: an act head needs joint fine-tuning (frozen backbone + head alone fails at synchrony), the fine-tune on a small paired corpus will cost speech quality unless mitigated, and the adaptation itself is cheap (1,700 steps).

findings.claim: MoshiVis adds visual input to a frozen 7B Moshi with 206M trainable parameters: cross-attention adapters between MHSA and FFN in every Temporal Transformer block, with cross-attention QKV projections shared across layers so image KV are cached once, and a self-gate (2-layer MLP, 1/8 hidden, sigmoid) that learns an unsupervised relevance score and can exactly recover base-model behaviour when zero.
findings.source_title: Vision-Speech Models: Teaching Speech Models to Converse about Images (MoshiVis), Kyutai
findings.numbers: 206M trainable params; backbone 7B + PaliGemma2 SigLIP ~400M frozen; 448 px -> 1024 image tokens; gate MLP hidden reduction 1/8 + sigmoid, unsupervised; OCR-VQA audio 63.7% no-gate -> 65.2% with gate; training 50k steps, batch 64, ~1 day on 8x H100; p_audio = 25% speech samples, rest 'speechless' image-text; MOSNet 2.78 with 0% audio -> 3.59 with 1% audio (base Moshi 3.34); VQAv2 zero-shot 49.3%.
findings.relevance: The template for Parcel's world-state conditioning: a gated adapter lets the model ignore the world stream when irrelevant (the 'only chuckle if funny / only look back if lost' requirement) while leaving the speech backbone frozen; the data-mixing trick shows speech quality survives with tiny amounts of paired audio.

findings.claim: MoshiVis's adapters add 7 ms per inference step on top of Moshi, giving roughly 51 ms/step at conversation start and 59 ms/step with a 5-minute context on an NVIDIA L4, inside the 80 ms frame budget of the 12.5 Hz codec; weights are CC-BY 4.0, code MIT/Apache-2.0.
findings.source_title: kyutai-labs/moshivis README and HF card kyutai/moshika-vis-pytorch-bf16
findings.numbers: +7 ms/step; 51 ms -> 59 ms/step (0 -> 5 min context) on L4; also runs on Mac Mini M4 Pro; PyTorch bf16 needs ~24 GB GPU; Q8_0 in Rust/MLX; licenses: Python MIT, Rust Apache-2.0, weights CC-BY 4.0, PaliGemma2 encoder Apache-2.0; HF card: 'research only'.
findings.relevance: Latency and licensing anchor for a conditioning adapter on Parcel; the 20 ms headroom on an L4 is the number Orin must be measured against.

findings.claim: MoshiRAG injects retrieved text into Moshi without any new token stream: the model emits a retrieval-trigger token in its inner-monologue text stream, retrieval runs asynchronously, and the reference embeddings are projected by one trainable linear layer and summed onto the Temporal Transformer input in streaming fashion; factuality jumps while turn-taking is preserved.
findings.source_title: MoshiRAG: Asynchronous Knowledge Retrieval for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models (TTI-Chicago / Kyutai / Gradium)
findings.numbers: HaluEval 36.3% vs 10.5%; TriviaQA 69.6% vs 22.8%; end-to-end keyword delay 3.1 s vs 2.1 s; target retrieval <= 2 s, 'sensitive to retrieval delays over 3 seconds'; takeover rate on pause track 0.32 vs 0.99; full fine-tune 100k updates, lr 2e-6, batch 32, reference encoder frozen; ~1.9M synthetic conversations; weights kyutai/moshika-rag-*-bf16 CC-BY 4.0, code MIT/Apache-2.0; 24 GB+ GPU plus encoder GPU.
findings.relevance: The cheapest injection template for a sparse world-event stream (track-loss, laughter score) and a precedent for a special 'act' token living in the text stream that triggers an asynchronous side process.

findings.claim: DyaPlex (NVIDIA/HKUST) is the closest published 'speech + body motion on one 12.5 Hz clock' system, but it is a dual-tower design: a frozen PersonaPlex speech tower plus a trainable 32-layer, d=1024 causal motion tower that cross-attends to all 32 speech-tower layers with time-aligned RoPE; motion is 22 RVQ codes per frame decoded one at a time, which costs 173 ms/frame at full context (80 ms at 1024-token motion context) on an RTX A6000 Ada; no code or weights released.
findings.source_title: DyaPlex: Full-Duplex Speech-Motion Model for Dyadic Interaction (NVIDIA)
findings.numbers: Motion tokenizer: causal body-part RVQ-VAE (GestureLSM-based), 25 fps SMPL-X -> 12.5 Hz, K=22 codes/frame (18 body + 4 face), vocab 4096; 46 tokens/frame in the motion tower (2 speakers); data Seamless Interaction 4,000 h -> 3,435 h filtered; 6x H100, 30k iters, batch 512, lr 3e-4; latency: audio tower 30 ms, RVQ decoder 0.8 ms, motion tower 173 ms/frame @4096 ctx -> 80 ms @1024 ctx (1.8 s); FGD 5.6e-3 vs A2P 57e-3; user study n=32: 97.5% vs DualTalk, 66.3% vs Audio2Photoreal; agent speech not conditioned on partner motion; authors suggest a 'Moshi-similar depth transformer design to speed up inference'.
findings.relevance: Shows that a per-frame autoregressive motion vocabulary of tens of codes cannot fit an 80 ms frame budget even on a desktop GPU; Parcel's act stream must be few tokens, non-AR (Moshi-Face style), and the frozen-speech-tower + cross-attention pattern is a viable fallback if joint fine-tuning proves too costly.

findings.claim: Hibiki reuses Moshi's multistream architecture for simultaneous speech translation (source audio in, target audio + text out at 12.5 Hz with 16 codebooks) and shows the architecture scales down to a 1.7B model that runs in real time on an iPhone 16 Pro; weights are CC-BY 4.0.
findings.source_title: High-Fidelity Simultaneous Speech-To-Speech Translation (Hibiki), Kyutai
findings.numbers: Temporal 2.2B (d 2560, 24 layers) + Depth 1.1B distilled to 449M; Hibiki-M 1.7B with 8 codebooks, real-time on iPhone 16 Pro; faster than real-time on H100 with 320 parallel sequences; ~40k h/language synthetic parallel data; 150k S2ST steps batch 96 + 8k fine-tune steps on ~900 h; CVSS-C ASR-BLEU 39.2 vs Seamless 37.0, speaker sim 0.41 vs 0.30, MOS 3.73 vs 2.18; end offset 2.9 s, LAAL 5.0 s; lag control by silence insertion, penalty 0 -> -2 over 1 -> 2 s lag; CFG gamma=3.0 lifts speaker sim 0.42 -> 0.48; GitHub: code MIT/Apache-2.0, weights CC-BY 4.0 (arXiv page's CC BY-NC-SA is the paper license).
findings.relevance: Evidence that the Moshi multistream design survives shrinking to 1-2B for on-device use, which matters if the 7B does not meet Orin's frame budget; the silence-insertion lag-control trick is a template for scheduling an act before or after speech.

findings.claim: Kyutai's moshi-finetune repo provides LoRA fine-tuning of Moshi's Temporal and Depth Transformers (rank <= 128, optional full embedding fine-tune) from stereo audio + timestamped transcripts at ~12k tokens/s on one H100 (39.6 GB), Apache-2.0; the base Moshi weights are CC-BY 4.0, 7B, Mimi 12.5 Hz at 1.1 kbps, 160 ms theoretical / ~200 ms practical latency on an L4, 24 GB+ GPU in bf16.
findings.source_title: kyutai-labs/moshi-finetune README (and kyutai-labs/moshi README)
findings.numbers: LoRA rank <= 128; 1 H100: ~12k tok/s, 39.6 GB; 8 H100: ~10.7k tok/s/GPU, 23.7 GB/GPU; example run 2,000 steps, batch 16, 100 s sequences ~30M tokens; data: left channel = Moshi, right = user, JSONL + timestamped JSON. Moshi README: 7B; Mimi 24 kHz -> 12.5 Hz, 1.1 kbps; 160 ms theoretical (80 ms frame + 80 ms acoustic delay), ~200 ms on L4; int4/int8/bf16; code MIT/Apache-2.0; weights CC-BY 4.0.
findings.relevance: The cost and tooling anchor for adding an act head: a Moshi-Face-scale adaptation (1,700 steps) is hours on one H100, and LoRA is the obvious mitigation for the UTMOS regression Moshi-Face saw with full fine-tuning.

findings.claim: PersonaPlex (NVIDIA, Jan 2026) is a Moshi-derived 7B full-duplex model released under the NVIDIA Open Model License permitting commercial use, trained on Fisher (<10k h real audio), with 0.170 s turn-taking and 0.240 s interruption-stop latency; it is the frozen speech tower DyaPlex builds on.
findings.source_title: nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1 model card
findings.numbers: 7B; initialised from Moshiko; Fisher Parts 1&2, 7,303 conversations up to 10 min, <10k h real audio; turn-taking 0.170 s; interruption 0.240 s; tested A100 80 GB (Ampere/Hopper); license NVIDIA Open Model License + CC-BY-4.0 components; code MIT.
findings.relevance: A commercially licensed Moshi variant with persona/voice control that a Parcel act head could sit on instead of Moshiko, and the base DyaPlex used for its frozen-tower design.

findings.claim: ASPIRin shows that RL on a full-duplex SLM should act on a coarse projected action space (speech-active vs silent) rather than raw tokens: GRPO with rule-based interactivity rewards on the projected space preserves semantics and cuts duplicate n-grams by over 50% versus standard GRPO, which otherwise causes generative collapse.
findings.source_title: ASPIRin: Action Space Projection for Interactivity-Optimized Reinforcement Learning in Full-Duplex Speech Language Models (Hung-yi Lee lab)
findings.numbers: Binary action projection (active speech vs inactive silence); GRPO with rule-based rewards balancing interruption and response latency; >50% reduction in duplicate n-grams vs standard GRPO; base model and code not stated in the abstract.
findings.relevance: Directly informs how Parcel should optimise 'chuckle if funny' and 'look back if lost' from a laughter/track-loss reward: apply RL to the projected act channel, not to the audio codebooks.

findings.claim: SoulX-Duplug is a plug-and-play, frame-synchronous state-prediction module (Qwen3-0.6B + frozen GLM-4-Voice tokenizer) that per 160 ms chunk emits ASR tokens then one of five user-state tokens, at 240 ms theoretical / 205-250 ms deployed latency, matching Moshi on turn-taking and beating it on pause handling on Full-Duplex-Bench; code is open-sourced.
findings.source_title: SoulX-Duplug: Plug-and-Play Streaming State Prediction Module for Realtime Full-Duplex Speech Conversation
findings.numbers: States: user_idle, user_nonidle, user_backchannel, user_complete, user_incomplete; chunk 160 ms; latency 80+160 = 240 ms theoretical, 205 ms EN / 250 ms bilingual deployed; turn-taking TOR 0.933 (Moshi 0.941, Freeze-Omni 0.336); pause TOR 0.352 (Moshi 0.983); interruption respond rate 0.83 vs Freeze-Omni 0.44; Easy-Turn 84.33%; state data 1,000 h Fisher + 10,000 h Mandarin; ASR data ~47k h Mandarin + ~31k h English; github.com/Soul-AILab/SoulX-Duplug, license not stated.
findings.relevance: A template for a small side head that turns a continuous observation into a discrete, timestamped event token (the 'observable track-loss event' Parcel needs) without touching the dialogue backbone.

findings.claim: Unmute (Kyutai) is a cascaded STT -> text-LLM -> TTS wrapper, not a Moshi stream extension: ~750 ms latency on one GPU (~450 ms on three), 16 GB VRAM, MIT code, and tool/function calling is explicitly 'not currently supported'.
findings.source_title: kyutai-labs/unmute README
findings.numbers: Kyutai STT + Kyutai TTS + Gemma 3 1B locally (GPT-OSS-120B via OpenRouter in production); ~750 ms single GPU, ~450 ms with three GPUs; 16 GB VRAM minimum; x86_64 Linux/WSL only; code MIT; tool calling not supported.
findings.relevance: Rules Unmute out as a template for a single-clock act stream; it is the 'wrap any LLM' fallback architecture with 2-4x the latency of Moshi-family models.

findings.claim: Full-Duplex-Bench-v3 benchmarks multi-step tool use for full-duplex voice agents on real disfluent human audio, but evaluates only API models and a cascade (no Moshi-family model), finding GPT-Realtime at Pass@1 0.600 and a cascade at 10.12 s latency versus 4.25 s for Gemini Live 3.1.
findings.source_title: Full-Duplex-Bench-v3: Benchmarking Tool Use for Full-Duplex Voice Agents Under Real-World Disfluency (Hung-yi Lee lab)
findings.numbers: Five disfluency categories; four task domains with chained API calls; GPT-Realtime Pass@1 0.600, 13.5% interruption rate; Gemini Live 3.1 latency 4.25 s, 78.0% turn-take; cascade (Whisper -> GPT-4o -> TTS) 10.12 s latency; CC BY-SA 4.0.
findings.relevance: Confirms that no open Moshi-family model has a published tool-use/action-emission mechanism; the 'act channel' for Parcel has to be designed from the Moshi-Face / DuplexSLA patterns rather than copied.

findings.claim: DuplexSLA represents actions as a rate-limited textual action channel decoded alongside assistant audio on a shared 160 ms chunk timeline (three channels: continuous user audio, discrete assistant audio, text actions) — the 'action as text on the clock' alternative to a learned act codebook.
findings.source_title: DuplexSLA: A Full-Duplex Spoken Language Model with Synchronized Speech, Language, and Action
findings.numbers: 160 ms chunk timeline; dual-stream three-channel formulation; action channel is rate-limited text; base model, vocabulary, latency and accuracy numbers not in the abstract (covered in the first sweep).
findings.relevance: The contrasting design choice for Parcel's act stream: sparse function-call text on the chunk clock (DuplexSLA) versus dense per-frame discrete codes (Moshi-Face/DyaPlex); the laugh/look-back behaviours are sparse events, which favours a small per-frame vocabulary with an explicit no-op.

design_implications: Act stream: copy Moshi-Face's structure — N small parallel tokens per 80 ms frame (they use N=8, K=256), fed back as inputs to the Temporal Transformer for both self and world/owner (2N in), emitted by a non-autoregressive side head conditioned on h_{i+1} + text + audio embeddings, delayed one step versus text. Use a hand-designed causal act vocabulary (gait, body yaw/pitch bins, vocalisation type, gaze target, explicit no-op) so no non-causal codec is needed; the head is one extra small forward pass per frame.

Do not use a per-frame autoregressive motion vocabulary: DyaPlex's 22 RVQ codes/frame cost 173 ms/frame at full context (80 ms at 1.8 s context) on an RTX A6000 Ada, above the 80 ms frame budget even before Orin; keep act tokens few and generated in parallel.

Plan for joint fine-tuning and its speech-quality tax: Moshi-Face's frozen-backbone ablation gave chance-level synchrony (LSE-D 11.8 vs random 11.7) while joint fine-tuning on 180 h halved UTMOS (3.08 -> 1.75; audio-only Moshi-ft 1.69). Mitigate with LoRA (moshi-finetune, rank <= 128), a head-only warm-up step (removing it worsened LSE-D 8.76 -> 9.53), and MoshiVis-style mixing where only ~25% of batches carry speech (speech quality recovered with as little as 1% audio).

World-state IN ('was the joke funny', 'is the owner tracked'): use MoshiVis-style gated cross-attention adapters (206M params, +7 ms/step, unsupervised sigmoid gate that can exactly recover base behaviour) for dense observations, and MoshiRAG-style one-linear-layer additive injection onto the Temporal Transformer input for sparse event streams; both leave the 7B frozen and preserved turn-taking.

Observable track-loss event: produce it with a SoulX-Duplug/X2-Turn-style frame-synchronous state head (five-state token per 160 ms chunk, ~240 ms latency) or an explicit input token, then feed it in as a world stream; MoshiRAG's trigger-token-in-inner-monologue pattern is the precedent for a token that launches an asynchronous side process.

Reward learning (owner laughter -> chuckle): follow ASPIRin and run GRPO on a coarse projected action space (chuckle / no-chuckle, look-back / continue) rather than on raw audio tokens, which caused generative collapse in standard GRPO.

Licensing: Moshi, MoshiVis, MoshiRAG, Hibiki weights are CC-BY 4.0 and moshi-finetune is Apache-2.0; PersonaPlex is NVIDIA Open Model License (commercial OK). Moshi-Face and DyaPlex ship no code or weights, so the act head must be reimplemented from the paper's Eq. 1-3 and training schedule (500 + 1,200 steps).

Latency is unmeasured on Orin for every source: MoshiVis is 51-59 ms/step on an L4 (~20 ms headroom), Moshi ~200 ms end-to-end on an L4, DyaPlex on an A6000 Ada. Measure a quantised Moshi + side-head step on the Orin before committing to a single 12.5 Hz clock; Hibiki-M (1.7B real-time on an iPhone 16 Pro) shows the multistream design survives shrinking to 1-2B if the 7B does not fit.

Data: 180 h of paired dialogue+behaviour sufficed for a synchronous face head (3,435 h for full-body dyadic motion); Parcel's paired (speech, act, world-state) corpus does not exist and must be synthesised or collected, with ground-truth act tokens available for teacher forcing across time (removing the t-1 act input hurt LSE-C and UTMOS).

results.claim: Moshi-Face adds facial motion as N=8 parallel discrete tokens per 12.5 Hz frame (codebook K=256, dim 128), read as input streams for both speakers (2N in) and generated for the system (N out) by a non-autoregressive 'Face Transformer' side head conditioned on the Temporal Transformer hidden state plus the frame's text and audio token embeddings — not as extra Depth-Transformer codebooks.
results.evidence_quote: "Face token streams (2N in, N out) ... The model reads 2N streams (system and user) and generates the N streams of the system's facial motion." / "The number of face components was set to N=8, and the codebook size was K=256 with an embedding dimension of C=128. To align the face tokens with Moshi's text and audio tokens encoded at 12.5 Hz, we set the temporal downsampling factor to r=2, such that the face codec encoded the input facial motion at 25 fps into face tokens at 12.5 Hz." / "Face Transformer. This module is a non-causal, transformer-based module that generates N face tokens at each timestep, conditioned on the outputs of RQ-Transformer. Since the N face tokens within each frame are quantized independently with no sequential dependency, they are generated non-autoregressively in parallel. At each timestep, the module first forms a unified conditioning vector by summing the hidden state with the text and audio token embeddings: e^All_{i+1} = h_{i+1} + e^0_{i+1} + sum_{m=1}^{M} e^m_i, (2) where e^0_{i+1} is the text token embedding, and e^m_i is the embedding of the m-th audio token, both produced by the embedding tables of the Face Transformer. This vector is then projected and combined with a learnable positional embedding pe^n to form a query ... for each of the N output positions. These query vectors are then passed through the Face Transformer, which applies non-causal self-attention across the N positions within each timestep, and N per-component linear heads predict the face tokens f^{1:N}_i in parallel" / "Following the implementation of Moshi, the audio and face token streams are delayed by one timestep relative to the text tokens" / "L_Moshi-Face = L_text + L_audio + lambda L_face" with "the face loss weight lambda=1" / Table 1 row "256 128 0.66 9.90 11.77" (MVE, LVE x10^-3). arXiv abs page: "Accepted to Interspeech 2026", authors Jiang, Ohashi, Higashinaka, Nagoya University.
results.correction: All numbers check out. Two wording nuances: (1) the paper calls h_{i+1} "the resulting hidden state" of the RQ-Transformer (Eq. 1: h_{i+1}, t_{i+1}, a_i^{1:M} = T_RQ(...)); it never says "Temporal Transformer hidden state" explicitly, though it does name "Temporal/Depth/Face Transformers" separately in the training section and the Depth Transformer is what emits the audio codebooks, so the reading is sound. (2) The paper does not explicitly argue against putting face tokens in the Depth Transformer; the contrast is implicit in the architecture (face tokens come from the separate Face Transformer; the Depth Transformer stays the audio-codebook generator). One extra detail worth carrying: in both training steps ground-truth face tokens from timestep i-1 are embedded and added to the query vectors (the 't-1 face token input' ablation), so the head also sees the previous frame's face tokens. The Face Transformer's layer count / hidden size / parameter count is indeed not reported anywhere in the HTML (0 hits for 'layers' or 'parameters').

results.claim: Moshi-Face was trained on ~180 h (~3,400 dialogues) of Seamless Interaction data with a two-step schedule (frozen Moshi + head, then joint full fine-tune); on LLM-judge dialogue metrics it matches original Moshi, but the 180 h fine-tune halves UTMOS speech naturalness (an effect the audio-only Moshi-ft control shares), and the frozen-backbone ablation gives chance-level lip sync — joint fine-tuning was 'essential'.
results.evidence_quote: "we randomly downloaded approximately 180 hours of dialogue data, totaling around 3,400 dialogues." / "We initialized the RQ-Transformer with the pre-trained Moshi checkpoint [https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16] and attached a randomly initialized Face Transformer. Training followed a two-step strategy: Step 1: The RQ-Transformer was frozen, and only the Face Transformer was trained; Step 2: All components were jointly fine-tuned. Step 1 used a learning rate of 5e-4, 500 training steps, and a batch size of 32. Step 2 used learning rates of 2e-6/4e-6/1e-5 for the Temporal/Depth/Face Transformers, with the face loss weight lambda=1, 1,200 training steps, and a batch size of 16." / Table 2 rows: "Moshi ... 3.08 3.76 3.73 4.26 3.85 | Moshi-ft ... 1.69 3.59 4.28 3.95 3.55 | Reconstructed face 8.53 0.12 | Random face 11.7 0.13 11.8 0.11 | Moshi-Face (Ours) 8.76 0.14 11.0 0.16 1.75 3.79 4.52 4.24 3.76 | w/o Face Transformer pre-training 9.53 0.13 10.4 0.14 1.71 3.78 4.53 4.25 3.76 | w/o full fine-tuning 11.8 0.16 11.1 0.20 2.42 3.24 3.94 3.89 3.23" / "Both Moshi-Face and Moshi-ft obtained lower UTMOS scores than the original Moshi, which is expected, given that fine-tuning on a smaller domain-specific dataset can degrade general speech quality. Notably, the ablation without full fine-tuning achieved a higher UTMOS than other Moshi-Face variants, as only training the Face Transformer preserves the original Moshi speech generation ability. Despite the lower UTMOS, Moshi-Face achieved the highest coherence and the second-highest naturalness in LLMAJ among all models, with overall quality comparable to Moshi." / "Removing full fine-tuning (Step 2) resulted in the worst LSE-D and lowest LLMAJ scores, demonstrating that joint fine-tuning is essential."
results.correction: Every number in the claim's numbers field matches Table 2 and the training section exactly. Three precision notes: (1) 'halves UTMOS' is an approximation — UTMOS drops from 3.08 to 1.75 (Moshi-Face, -43%) and 1.69 (Moshi-ft, -45%); say 'cuts UTMOS by roughly 45%'. (2) 'chance-level lip sync' is the checker's reading of the numbers (w/o full FT teacher-forced LSE-D 11.8 vs the Random-face lower bound 11.7; free-run 11.1 vs 11.8); the paper itself only says 'worst LSE-D'. (3) 'No GPU reported' should be 'no GPU type/count or wall-clock reported' — the acknowledgments do say 'We used the computational resources of the supercomputer Flow at the Information Technology Center, Nagoya University.' No latency figures and no code/weights/demo release statement appear anywhere in the paper (0 hits for 'release', 'available', 'code'); the only link is to the base Moshi checkpoint.

results.claim: MoshiVis adds visual input to a frozen 7B Moshi with 206M trainable parameters: cross-attention adapters between MHSA and FFN in every Temporal Transformer block, with cross-attention QKV projections shared across layers so image KV are cached once, and a self-gate (2-layer MLP, 1/8 hidden, sigmoid) that learns an unsupervised relevance score and can exactly recover base-model behaviour when zero.
results.evidence_quote: "As backbones, we use Moshi [8] for the speech modality (~7B parameters), and the 'stage 2' vision encoder of PaliGemma [5] (~400M parameters) for images. Both backbones are kept frozen during training, and we only train the adaptation modules (~206M parameters)." / "The image tokens are injected into the current speech token via residual cross-attention (CA) layers, placed between the multi-head self attention (MHSA) and the feedforward network (FFN) in every transformer block. As the cross-attention's QKV projections are shared across layers, at inference, we only need to compute the keys and values once per image, thus reducing the memory cost needed to store the image embeddings." / "we further modulate the output of the cross-attention module with a self-gating mechanism. Intuitively, a gate output of zero would turn off the image information and exactly recover the base model behaviour, while higher values facilitate the flow of image information. Specifically, the gate is a small 2-layer MLP with a hidden size reduction factor of 1/8, followed by a sigmoid activation. During training, we do not supervise the gate's outputs and instead let it implicitly learn an image relevance score for each token." / "our model exactly recovers the backbone speech transformer when the gates' outputs are all zeros." / Table 4 (OCR-VQA, audio eval): gate none 63.7; shared gate + shared QKV 65.2. / "trained for 50k steps with batch size 64, taking roughly one day of training on 8 x H100 GPUs." / Table 1: "p_audio 0% 1% 5% 10% Moshi | MOSNet 2.78 3.59 3.47 3.56 3.34" / "a ratio of p_audio=25% appears to be a good trade-off" / "when trained with p_audio=0% and prompted in the audio domain, the model yields 38.5% on OCR-VQA, 49.3% on VQAv2".
results.correction: Claim holds. Minor terminology: the paper says the CA layers sit 'in every transformer block' of the 7B speech transformer and never uses the phrase 'Temporal Transformer' (it describes the depth transformer as a separate, unmodified audio-codebook decoder), so 'every Temporal Transformer block' is a Moshi-paper paraphrase, not the MoshiVis wording. The 63.7% -> 65.2% OCR-VQA pair is specifically 'no gate' vs 'gate shared across layers + QKV shared' (the deployed config); the un-shared-gate + shared-KV cell is 66.2%. The encoder is described as the PaliGemma 'stage 2' vision encoder (~400M); the README adds it is the PaliGemma2 encoder from google/paligemma2-3b-pt-448 — 'SigLIP' is not named in the paper. The 49.3% VQAv2 number is the p_audio=0% model prompted in audio, which the paper does not label 'zero-shot'.

results.claim: MoshiVis's adapters add 7 ms per inference step on top of Moshi, giving roughly 51 ms/step at conversation start and 59 ms/step with a 5-minute context on an NVIDIA L4, inside the 80 ms frame budget of the 12.5 Hz codec; weights are CC-BY 4.0, code MIT/Apache-2.0.
results.evidence_quote: README (kyutai-labs/moshivis): "The present code is provided under the MIT license for the Python parts, and Apache license for the Rust backend"; "All model weights (excluding the bundled vision encoder) are released under the CC-BY 4.0 license"; "the vision encoder is licensed under Apache 2.0"; "In total, MoshiVis adds ~206M adapters parameters on top of the 7B Moshi"; "you will need a GPU with a significant amount of memory (~24GB)"; "A MLX version (tested on a MacBook Pro M3)". The README contains NO occurrence of 'ms', 'latency' figures, 'L4', or 'M4'. The latency numbers are in the paper (arXiv 2503.15633, Sec. 4.3): "On an NVIDIA L4 GPU, for images of 448 pixels (1024 tokens) and an 8-bit quantized model, MoshiVis requires roughly 7 extra milliseconds of runtime per inference step compared to the backbone model, for a total of 51ms per step at the beginning of the conversation and 59ms with a 5-minute context window. ... the model is well within the 80ms threshold for real-time latency (the audio codec having a frequency of 12.5Hz)." Kyutai blog (kyutai.org/moshivis): "MoshiVis adds only about ~7ms of latency per inference step", "for a total of 55ms per inference step", "staying well below the 80ms second limit of real-time latency", "on a consumer-grade device (MacMini with M4 Pro Chip)". HF card kyutai/moshika-vis-pytorch-bf16: license "cc-by-4.0"; "This model is for research only and we do not recommend it for providing advices or to perform any professionnal duty."
results.correction: The statements are true but misattributed and missing one qualifier. Corrected: 'Per the MoshiVis paper (arXiv 2503.15633, Sec. 4.3) — not the GitHub README, which carries no latency figures — the adapters add roughly 7 ms per inference step for an 8-bit quantized model with 448 px images (1024 tokens) on an NVIDIA L4, for a total of 51 ms/step at conversation start and 59 ms/step with a 5-minute context window, within the 80 ms budget of the 12.5 Hz codec (the Kyutai blog rounds this to ~7 ms extra / 55 ms total). Per the README, Python code is MIT, the Rust backend Apache-2.0, model weights CC-BY 4.0 excluding the Apache-2.0 PaliGemma2 vision encoder; PyTorch bf16 needs ~24 GB with no quantization support; the MLX build was tested on a MacBook Pro M3 (the Mac Mini M4 Pro demo is from the blog, not the README); the HF card says research only.' Note the 51/59 ms numbers are for the Q8 Rust backend, so a bf16 PyTorch deployment would not inherit them, and the '20 ms headroom' figure should be quoted as L4 + Q8 specific.

sweeps.topic: Local, permissively licensed laughter / non-verbal vocalization synthesis for the dog's chuckle and simulated owner reactions; laughter datasets to augment the owner-laughter detector

findings.claim: Orpheus TTS (Apache-2.0, Llama-3B backbone, tags <laugh> <chuckle> <sigh> <cough> <sniffle> <groan> <yawn> <gasp>) is the best open tag-based laughter TTS in the only head-to-head benchmark: NVBench NVV F1 0.728 vs CosyVoice 2 0.463, Dia 0.632, Bark 0.654, Fish-Speech 0.432, Higgs-Audio 0.382; subjective NVV accuracy 3.71/5.
findings.source_title: NVBench / NVV-SuperBench: Benchmarking Nonverbal Vocalizations in Speech Generation

findings.claim: Even the best open models misrender non-verbal tags most of the time: NV-Bench paralinguistic CER on English is 71.92% for Orpheus-TTS and 62.75% for CosyVoice3; a laughter-specialised fine-tune (NV-CV3) still gets 46.13% overall and 27.69% on Mandarin laughter (CosyVoice3 57.69%). Synthesized laughs must be verified by a detector rather than trusted from the tag.

findings.source_title: Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 model card (+ CosyVoice 3 paper arXiv 2505.17589, CosyVoice GitHub)

findings.claim: A fully permissive detector-augmentation path exists: VocalSound is CC BY-SA 4.0 with 3,504 laughter clips (21,024 total, 3,365 speakers), and adding it to FSD50K raised laughter F1 0.45->0.59 (+29.7%) and overall mAP +41.9%.

Code is MIT but the released weights are research-only.

findings.claim: AudioSet's Laughter class (5,696 clips: Baby 863, Giggle 991, Snicker 1,857, Belly laugh 843, Chuckle/chortle 1,693) is released under CC BY 4.0 (labels; audio fetched from YouTube IDs), giving in-the-wild negatives/positives to pair with VocalSound.

findings.numbers: Laughter 5,696; children 863/991/1,857/843/1,693; dataset CC BY 4.0, ontology CC BY-SA 4.0; splits eval 20,383, balanced 22,176, unbalanced 2,042,985 segments; 128-d 1 Hz features 2.4 GB

findings.claim: Dia-1.6B (Apache-2.0, English only) has the widest open tag set (21 tags incl. (laughs) (chuckle)) but warns they 'might result in unexpected output', and on an A4000 generates 40 tok/s against 86 tok/s per second of audio, i.e. about 2x slower than real time; NVBench WER 21.95.
findings.source_title: nari-labs/Dia-1.6B-0626 model card (+ Dia2 GitHub)
findings.numbers: 1.6B; Apache 2.0; English only; ~10 GB VRAM; A4000 40 tok/s, 86 tok/s = 1 s audio; Dia2 1B/2B Apache 2.0, English, no NV tag list
findings.relevance: Useful for offline English owner-dialogue simulation with laughs; not an Orin or Korean option

findings.claim: The only open laughter-only synthesizer is the 2023 pseudo-phonetic-token method on Laughterscape (HuBERT k-means 200 tokens -> FastSpeech2 -> HiFi-GAN): MOS 3.00 vs ground truth 3.73 vs ASR-phoneme baseline 1.25; unconditional laughter MOS 3.11. Code MIT, but the Laughterscape corpus (6.04 h, 11,413 laughs, 584 Japanese speakers) is 'Research and development purpose only (tentative)'.
findings.source_title: Laughter Synthesis using Pseudo Phonetic Tokens with a Large-scale In-the-wild Laughter Corpus (Interspeech 2023) + corpus site + GitHub
findings.numbers: corpus v1.0 6.04 h / 11,413 utt / 584 speakers / 24 kHz (paper: 3.5 h, 7,489 utt, 470 speakers); MOS GT 3.73, HiFi-GAN 3.31, baseline 1.25, Proposed-L5 3.00, SMOS L12 3.22, MCD 11.41, F0-RMSE 80.28; unconditional MOS 3.11 SMOS 2.65; vocoder 1.5 weeks on V100; ASR baseline failed 6.9%

findings.claim: NVSpeech / Emilia-NV provides 573 h of Mandarin with word-level [Laughter] and 17 other paralinguistic tags and CosyVoice2 fine-tunes reaching tag recall up to 61.9%, but the dataset is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the human-annotated 48k subset is private; NonverbalTTS (17 h English, VoxCeleb+Expresso, Apache-2.0) is the one permissive NV fine-tuning corpus found.
findings.source_title: NVSpeech: An Integrated and Scalable Pipeline for Human-Like Speech Modeling with Paralinguistic Vocalizations (+ HF amphion/Emilia-NV, deepvk/NonverbalTTS)

findings.claim: Preference optimization on CosyVoice2-0.5B with an NV-aware CER cut single-tag NV-CER from 3.62 to 2.59 and won 55.5% vs 44.5% human preference on NV accuracy, showing DPO on a 0.5B TTS is the cheap lever for tag fidelity (no code/weights released).
findings.source_title: Preference Optimization for Non-Verbal Vocalization Synthesis
findings.numbers: Emilia-NV 573.4 h, 18 tags; SFT NV-CER 3.62 -> DPO 2.59; preference 55.5/44.5 (NV acc), 57.2/42.8 (lexical acc); no per-type laughter split

findings.claim: Bark (MIT) is the only other permissive model with both Korean and a [laughter] tag, but it needs ~12 GB VRAM, is only 'roughly real-time' on enterprise GPUs, and scores NVBench WER 14.73 with coverage 0.11.
findings.source_title: suno-ai/bark
findings.numbers: MIT; 13 languages incl. Korean; tags [laughter] [laughs] [sighs] [music] [gasps] [clears throat]; 12 GB VRAM (8 GB small models); NVBench F1 0.654, WER 14.73, cov 0.11

findings.source_title: jetson-containers issue #532 (Jetson AI Lab MLC benchmarks) + Baseten/Simplismart Orpheus pages + maya-research/maya1 card
findings.numbers: Orpheus real-time bar ~83 tok/s (Baseten) / ~91 tok/s (Simplismart), H100 TTFB ~130 ms; AGX Orin published Llama2-7B 47 tok/s, Gemma 75; user 32 GB ~19/~23; Orin Nano Super Llama 3.2 3B 27.7->43.07 tok/s; Maya1 3B Apache 2.0, 16 GB+ VRAM, vLLM sub-100 ms, English only
findings.relevance: Justifies the two-tier plan: 3B tag-TTS on the desktop, sub-1B or pre-rendered clips on the robot

design_implications: Two-tier synthesis: generate the dog's chuckle bank and simulated owner laughs offline on the RTX 5000 Ada with Orpheus TTS (Apache-2.0, NVBench F1 0.728); on the Orin play pre-rendered clips, or if live TTS is required use Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B (Apache-2.0, [laughter], 150 ms) or Chatterbox-Turbo (MIT, [laugh]); do not plan on a 3B SNAC-TTS running in real time on AGX Orin (needs 83-91 tok/s, NVIDIA's 7B int4 number is 47 tok/s).

Never trust a laughter tag: best open PCER is 46-72% (NV-Bench). Gate every synthesized laugh with the laughter detector (optionally NVMOS) before it enters the vocalization bank, and define the simulated-owner reward on detector output rather than on the tag so sim and real reward channels agree.

Korean owner audio for the simulator: Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B is the only Apache-2.0 Korean + [laughter] model; test Orpheus 3b-ko-ft-research_release (Apache-2.0, tags undocumented); Bark (MIT) is the fallback; Fish/OpenAudio, Breeze-TTS-2, IndexTTS and Higgs TTS 3 are excluded by license, Higgs Audio v2 only under its 100k-AAU community license.

Retrain the owner-laughter detector with the Omine recipe (MIT code) on VocalSound (CC BY-SA 4.0, 3,504 laughs) + AudioSet Laughter (CC BY 4.0, 5,696 clips): ~75 min on one GPU, expected detection F1 0.78-0.94 and onset MAE 0.31-1.09 s; use the retrained weights, not Omine's research-only release. Onset accuracy is the metric that matters for the 'chuckle if funny' timing reward.

If stock tags are insufficient, fine-tune/DPO the 0.5B on-robot TTS: NonverbalTTS (Apache-2.0, 17 h English) is the only permissive NV corpus; Emilia-NV (573 h Mandarin) is CC BY-NC-SA; the Aug-2026 DPO result (NV-CER 3.62 -> 2.59 on CosyVoice2-0.5B) shows the lever works at that size.

A laugh-only generator is optional: the 2023 pseudo-phonetic-token pipeline (MIT code) retrained on VocalSound would give a permissive non-speech dog vocalization (MOS ~3/5 by analogy); no 2025-26 open laughter-only generator exists, so Orpheus <laugh>/<chuckle> clips post-filtered by the detector are the default.

Open items to close with a quick test rather than more reading: whether Orpheus Korean checkpoints honour <laugh>; actual tok/s of a 3B SNAC-TTS on AGX Orin 64 GB; KsponSpeech/AI Hub license text for Korean in-context laughter.

results.evidence_quote: Table 3 (EN): "Orpheus TTS | EN | 4.98 ±0.34 | … | 0.18 | 0.687 ±0.026 | 0.774 ±0.034 | 0.728 ±0.029"; CosyVoice 2 F1 0.463±0.024; Dia 0.632±0.008; Bark 0.654±0.041; Fish-Speech 0.432±0.024; Higgs-Audio 0.382±0.050; ChatTTS 0.664±0.167; ElevenLabs 0.720±0.024. Table 4: Orpheus EN NVV Accuracy 3.71±2.46. Text: "In EN, strong correctness is not concentrated in a single system. Orpheus TTS delivers the strongest correctness profile, achieving the best precision and F1 together with competitive recall and low NTD." But: "ElevenLabs ranks best overall across languages in subjective listening tests… together with the strongest NVV perceptual effect, correctness, and overall expressiveness." and "Orpheus and CosyVoice2 sit in the mid-coverage tier with uneven per-type distinctiveness." Title is "NVBench: A Benchmark for Speech Synthesis with Non-Verbal Vocalizations" ("NVV-SuperBench" does not appear). Orpheus GitHub README: "Apache-2.0 license"; "built on the Llama-3b backbone"; tags "<laugh>, <chuckle>, <sigh>, <cough>, <sniffle>, <groan>, <yawn>, <gasp>"; "trained on 100k+ hours of English speech data"; "~200ms streaming latency".
results.correction: All numbers check out, and Orpheus has the best EN precision/F1 among all eight tag-based systems (including commercial ElevenLabs, 0.720). Three details are off: (1) it is NOT the only head-to-head benchmark — NV-Bench (arXiv 2603.15352) also compares Orpheus head-to-head and ranks it last on paralinguistic CER (71.92%); (2) the 0.728 F1 is aggregated over NVBench's 45-type NVV taxonomy in English, not a laughter-specific score (in ZH ChatTTS 0.703 beats Orpheus 0.625, and the paper notes ChatTTS's ZH lead is inflated by laugh dominance); (3) subjectively ElevenLabs, not Orpheus, ranks best overall. The Apache-2.0 / Llama-3B / tag list facts come from the Orpheus GitHub README, not from the paper, and the paper's name is NVBench (no 'NVV-SuperBench').

Synthesized laughs must be verified by a detector rather than trusted from the tag.
results.evidence_quote: Table 4 "Detailed performance on each subsets of NV-Bench", English single-label PCER: Orpheus-TTS 71.92, CosyVoice3 62.75, Emilia-NV-CV2 55.30, SMIIP-NV-CV2 56.80, NV-FlexiVoice 50.43, NV-CV3 46.13. Mandarin single-label PCER: SMIIP-NV-CV2 75.64, Emilia-NV-CV2 40.00, CosyVoice3 57.69, NV-FlexiVoice 31.08, NV-CV3 27.69. Text: "NV-CV3 achieves the lowest PCER (27.69%) and OCER (4.90%) on the Mandarin single-label subset". "Single-label Subset: A strictly balanced testset where each utterance contains exactly one NV event (50 samples per category, 650 Mandarin and 350 English utterances in total)". "NV-CV3: We finetune CV3 on a consolidated corpus comprising Emilia-NV, SMIIP-NV, NVTTS, Disfluency, and NVS." "This process yields a dataset of 1,651 prompt and GT pairs (7.9 hours)"; "14 NV types"; "License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0". No per-type (laughter) results table exists in the HTML paper.
results.correction: The English PCER numbers (Orpheus 71.92%, CosyVoice3 62.75%, NV-CV3 46.13%) are correct, but 46.13% is the English single-label figure, not an 'overall' one. The 27.69% / 40.00% / 57.69% values are PCER on the entire Mandarin single-label subset (all Mandarin NV categories, 50 utterances each), NOT a Mandarin-laughter score — the paper reports no per-type laughter numbers. NV-CV3 is not laughter-specialised: it is CosyVoice3 fine-tuned on a consolidated general nonverbal corpus (Emilia-NV, SMIIP-NV, NVTTS, Disfluency, NVS). The 'verify with a detector' recommendation is the author's own inference; the paper does not make it.

results.claim: Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 is the only Apache-2.0 model that combines Korean, an explicit [laughter]/[breath] tag, and sub-1B size with 150 ms bi-streaming latency; the CosyVoice 3 paper documents the tags but provides no evaluation of them.
results.evidence_quote: Model card: license "apache-2.0"; 0.5B; 9 languages "Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian" plus 18 Chinese dialects/accents; table "Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 | test-zh CER 1.21 / SS 78.0 | test-en WER 2.24 / SS 71.8", "_RL | 0.81 / 77.4 | 1.68 / 69.5"; code example uses "[breath]" with "for supported control, check cosyvoice/tokenizer/tokenizer.py#L280". tokenizer.py special tokens: "'[breath]', '', '', '[noise]', '[laughter]', '[cough]', … '', '', '[sigh]' …". GitHub README: "achieves latency as low as 150ms while maintaining high-quality audio output"; "Using TensorRT-LLM to accelerate cosyvoice2 llm could give 4x acceleration comparing with huggingface transformers implementation." Paper (2505.17589): "markers such as '[laughter]' and '[breath]' in the input text can be used to generate a noticeable laughter and breath, respectively"; "training data of CosyVoice 3 reaches one million hours"; "the text-to-speech LM is increased from 0.5B to 1.5B parameters"; no metric or listening test for the tags; "For Korean, the CER is approximately 6%, mainly due to the limited volume and quality of available data."
results.correction: The model-card facts (Apache-2.0, 0.5B, Korean among 9 languages, WER/CER/SS numbers, [breath]/[laughter] control tokens via tokenizer.py), the README's 150 ms bi-streaming figure, and the statement that the CosyVoice 3 paper documents '[laughter]'/'[breath]' without evaluating them are all confirmed. Two corrections: the 'only Apache-2.0 model that combines…' uniqueness claim is not made by any source and was not verified (no source surveys competitors); and the TensorRT-LLM '4x' is stated in the README for the CosyVoice 2 LLM, not for CosyVoice 3. Also note the paper's caveat that Korean CER is ~6% due to limited Korean data — material for a Korean-owner use case.

Paper (arXiv 2205.03433) Table 1: "Laughter … VocalSound 3,504" (each of six classes 3,504; "Vocal Sound Total … 21,024"). "collected from 3,365 speakers from 60 countries, with their ages ranging from 18 to 80"; "45% are female, 55% are male"; "The mean, median, and standard deviation of the audio length is 4.18s, 3.72s, and 1.81s, respectively. The audios are recorded at 44.1kHz"; split "15570 (74%), 1860 (9%), and 3594 (17%)"; "90.5±0.2%". Table 3 (FSD50K eval): Laughter F1 0.45 -> 0.59 (Improvement 29.7%), AP 0.46 -> 0.54 (18.1%); Vocal Classes Overall Avg. F1 31.8%, mAP 0.41 -> 0.59 (41.9%); text: "a relative f1-score improvement of 31.8% and an average precision improvement of 41.9%". Caveat: "the audio samples are not produced spontaneously but acted by the subjects".
results.correction: No correction needed. Minor precision: the +41.9% is the relative mAP gain over the four FSD50K vocal classes (laughter, sigh, cough, sneeze) in the 4+1-class setup, and the license appears in the GitHub README while the counts/metrics come from the arXiv paper.

sweeps.topic: Duplex speech-model licenses (Moshi / PersonaPlex / rl-seamless cards) and open full-duplex or streaming speech-to-speech models under 4B parameters (2025-2026), incl. Korean coverage

findings.claim: The Moshi base checkpoints are CC-BY-4.0 with no non-commercial clause, in every precision (bf16, q8, and mlx q4), so they are the only fully unrestricted native full-duplex weights in the family.

design_implications: Build Design A only on CC-BY-4.0 Moshi weights (moshiko/moshika bf16, q8, mlx q4) or NVIDIA-OML PersonaPlex-7B-v1; never on moshika-rl-seamless or personaplex-rl-seamless (CC BY-NC 4.0 via the Seamless Interaction dataset). If the RL interactivity gains are wanted, re-run the GRPO recipe on Fisher/synthetic/own data.

There is no downloadable sub-4B native full-duplex dialogue model with a permissive license as of 2026-08-28 (Kyutai has none below 7B; SALM-Duplex 1.1B has no weights). A small on-board dog brain means training one: Moshi-architecture at 1-3B (Hibiki-1B/Zero-3B prove the decoder size) or SALM-Duplex in NeMo, on a Parcel-made time-aligned synthetic corpus.

If 7B Moshi q8 fails the Orin benchmark, the fallback is a cascaded 'micro-turn' design: LFM2-Audio-1.5B (turn-based, <100 ms first audio, LFM Open License below US$10M revenue) driven by an always-on listener (laughter detector, track-loss event) that interrupts it, in the DuplexCascade pattern.

Korean is not available in any open duplex model (Raon-SpeechChat duplex is English-only and NC; HyperCLOVAX-SEED-Omni-8B is ASR/TTS/S2ST only; Kanana-o is API-only; Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B is Apache with Korean speech I/O but 35B/78 GB+). Plan for an English-speaking dog voice with a Korean ASR/TTS side-car, or budget for own Korean duplex training evaluated on KVoiceBench/KOpenAudioBench.

Every permissive native-duplex model is 7B-13B (Moshi, PersonaPlex, MiniCPM-o 4.5 TDM 9B, Lychee-FD 13B), so the Orin feasibility benchmark of Moshi q8 at 12.5 Hz remains the gating experiment before any architecture commitment.

NVIDIA OML is revocable and terminates on 'bypass ... any technical limitation, safety guardrail'; document that Parcel's motor safety layer sits outside the model so it cannot be read as a guardrail bypass, and ship the required NVIDIA notice if PersonaPlex is used.
