sweeps.topic: XVF3800 audio front end reality (AEC reference path, ERLE, DoA, channel formats, reSpeaker firmware variants) and ego-noise on legged robots (levels, spectra, detection degradation, suppression)

findings.claim: The XVF3800 AEC reference is the far-end stream the host sends TO the device on the left (0) channel of the USB/I2S input; the device's own I2S-master DAC plays that same channel to the speaker. There is no external-reference mode: robot speech played through any other speaker (e.g. the Go2's built-in one) is not cancelled.
findings.source_title: XMOS XVF3800 Datasheet, release 3.2.1 (section 3.4.3 Reference Signal for AEC; Table 3.1 Pipeline parameters)
findings.numbers: AEC: full duplex, mono; tail length 192 ms; reference channels 1 mono (output to DAC); reference bulk delay 0-500 ms (fixed); double-talk detection continuous; frequency range 80 Hz-8 kHz; pipeline 16 kHz; 4 PDM mics, alignment +/-2 dB; noise suppression 'up to 25 dB depending on input SNR'; 3 beams (2 focused + 1 scanning), 360 deg; beamformer update time 16 ms; input delay min 58 ms (mic in to I2S out); output delay typ 50 ms; operating distance 0.3-5 m; AGC 60 dB range; USB/I2S 16 or 48 kHz (build-time), USB 16/24/32-bit; core power 345 mW (I2S) / 400 mW (USB). No ERLE dB figure and no DoA accuracy figure are published.
findings.relevance: Decides the speaker wiring for Parcel: all TTS must be routed through the reSpeaker's own JST/3.5 mm output for echo cancellation; also fixes the ~60-110 ms front-end latency budget for the duplex clock.

findings.claim: AEC convergence needs several seconds of far-end audio, the device over-suppresses near-end speech until converged, and the Path Change Detector applies 'heavy near-end suppression during far-end activity' whenever the acoustic path changes (e.g. the device moves) — which is the normal state of a walking robot. ERLE is used only qualitatively (PCD thresholds), never as a published dB spec.
findings.source_title: XMOS XVF3800 User Guide, release 3.2.1 (sections 2.5.4 AEC Convergence, 3.5 DoA, 3.6.1 Output selection, 4.2.13 PCD, 8 ASR output)
findings.numbers: Convergence 'a few seconds', tuning procedure expects '< 30 seconds'; AEC_PCD_MINTHR default 0.02, AEC_PCD_MAXTHR default 0.2, AEC_PCD_COUPLINGI in [0,1] (outside range disables PCD); AEC_AECPATHCHANGE=1 while output is heavily suppressed. DoA: AEC_AZIMUTH_VALUES = 4 floats in radians (focused 1, focused 2, free-running, auto-select); AEC_SPENERGY_VALUES = 4 floats (>0 means speech); AUDIO_MGR_SELECTED_AZIMUTHS = 2 values, first is NAN when no speech; free-running beam 'can also pick up any noise signals present'. Output mux categories 0-12 incl. raw mics (1), far-end reference (4/5/12), processed beams (6: 0,1 slow, 2 fast, 3 auto-select), AEC residual/ASR (7). ASR output is post-beamformer with 'no noise suppression'; recommended -52 dBov for 61 dBSPL, AEC_ASROUTGAIN ~36 dB below PP_AGCGAIN. Mic HPF corner 70/125/150/180 Hz. Eval kit stops after 8 h; 'Licensed production XVF3800 devices do not have this restriction'. DFU tool GPLv2; DSP under proprietary XCORE VocalFusion Licence.
findings.relevance: Predicts that owner barge-in during robot-speech-plus-locomotion will be suppressed by the AEC/PCD; gives the exact commands for a speech-gated owner bearing ('look back when lost') and the channel to feed a learned front end (ASR channel).

findings.claim: The reSpeaker XVF3800 USB board is a 66 mm square 4-mic array with its own TLV320AIC3104 codec, 3.5 mm jack and 5 W JST speaker output, exposed as a UAC 2.0 device; the 6-channel USB firmware exposes Conference + ASR + 4 raw mics at 16 kHz/32-bit, and Seeed's DOA_VALUE returns an integer 0-359 degree bearing plus a VAD flag.
findings.source_title: Seeed Studio Wiki — Getting Started with reSpeaker XVF3800 USB Mic Array (plus the Python SDK page and the respeaker GitHub firmware folder/changelog)
findings.numbers: Mic geometry (m): (0.033,-0.033), (0.033,0.033), (-0.033,0.033), (-0.033,-0.033); 360 deg far-field to 5 m; 60 dB AGC; 12 WS2812 LEDs. Firmware: usb v2.0.x 2-ch (Ch0 Conference, Ch1 ASR, 16 kHz 32-bit); 6chl (Ch2-5 raw mics 0-3); i2s v1.0.x 2-ch 32-bit; i2s master 48k (Home Assistant). Repo files include respeaker_xvf3800_usb_dfu_firmware_v2.1.0.bin, _v2.1.0_16k6ch.bin, _v2.1.0_48k2ch.bin, _6chl_v2.0.8.bin, _v2.0.9_48k.bin. Changelog: v2.0.6 added read-only DOA_VALUE (0-359 deg); v2.0.8 added profile 'ua-io16-6ch-sqr' six-channel 16 kHz capture; v2.0.10 decoupled DOA state from LED effect; v2.1.0 added AUDIO_MGR_OP_CH3-6 routing and AIC3104 HP/line-out level commands, default 8 dB. Python SDK example polls DOA_VALUE every 0.1 s. CNX Software: mic sensitivity -26 dBFS, AOP 120 dB SPL, SNR 64 dBA, max sample rate 16 kHz, $49.99/$54.50.
findings.relevance: Fixes the firmware choice (v2.1.0_16k6ch) for Parcel: raw mics for custom ego-noise processing plus the ASR channel for the model, and the integer-degree DoA + VAD for the yaw target.

findings.claim: On a Unitree Go1 EDU walking at 0.5 m/s, a sound-pressure sensor 30 cm above ground (about 50 cm from the foot contact point) measures 72-79 dBA mean and 81-84 dBA peak; the stationary fan floor is about 55 dBA; foot-ground impact, not motor whine, is the dominant source; a contact-velocity-shaped RL gait cuts about 8 dBA (2.5x sound pressure).
findings.source_title: MUTE — Minimizing Acoustic Noise: Enhancing Quiet Locomotion for Quadruped Robots in Indoor Applications (IROS 2025)
findings.numbers: Stationary, fan only: ~55 dBA. At 0.5 m/s, MNL/PNL dBA: DreamWaQ wood 73.51/83.18, carpet 71.90/80.80, tiles 72.34/80.93, avg 72.58/81.64; built-in MPC avg 79.01/82.80; MUTE beta=0 avg 68.91/76.52; MUTE beta=1 wood 65.78/73.18, carpet 62.48/69.52, tiles 66.15/76.22, avg 64.80/72.97; avg reduction ~8 dBA = 2.5x pressure. Office course 91.7 m at 0.36 m/s: MNL 68.25, PNL 76.8 dBA. Sensor 30 cm above ground, 20 Hz update.
findings.relevance: The closest thing to an on-body noise level for the Go2 class: sets the mic-side SNR during locomotion (roughly -10 to -25 dB against 55-65 dB SPL speech), far below the regimes where published ego-noise suppression works, and shows a quiet/stop-to-listen gait is the cheapest SNR gain.

findings.claim: Unitree Go2 running is about 70 dB at 0.5 m and 63-70 dB at 1 m, dropping to about 54 dB at 5 m in a bedroom — comparable to the 70 dB robot-vacuum level that bothers sensitive listeners; the wheeled Stretch is 15-18 dB quieter.
findings.source_title: ANAVI: Audio Noise Awareness using Visuals of Indoor environments for NAVIgation (CoRL 2024)
findings.numbers: Table 1 (apartment bedroom): Go2 running 70 dB @0.5 m S, 63 dB @1 m N, 54 dB @5 m W; Stretch 52/49/47 dB. Table 2 (house bedroom): Go2 69.7 dB @1m-west, 67.1 @1m-south, 66.1 @1m-south-1m-east (no LOS), 67.3 @2m-north, 66.7 @2m-south, 61.1 @2m-north-2m-west (no LOS), 65.4 @3m-west, 65.4 @3m-south; Stretch 54.2/52.1/49.7/51.7/50.5/45.3/48.6/48.2. Caveat: levels are re-radiated (recorded robot audio replayed through a laptop speaker, phones as receivers).
findings.relevance: Only Go2-specific level found; confirms the Go-class quadruped is a ~70 dB source at conversational distance.

findings.claim: Calibrated on-robot measurements: Go1 emits 74 dBA at ~15 cm, described as 'impulsive impact sound for every step combined with a high-frequency electric motor whirring'; Turtlebot 2i 72 dBA at ~10 cm; HSR 57 dBA at ~10 cm. Humans localize the Go1 sound to ~9.4-9.8 deg mean absolute error.
findings.source_title: Auditory Localization and Assessment of Consequential Robot Sounds: A Multi-Method Study in Virtual Reality (arXiv 2504.00697)
findings.numbers: GRAS 64AE 1/2-inch mics + HEAD acoustics SQobold mounted on each robot; Go1 74 dBA @ ~15 cm; Turtlebot 72 dBA @ ~10 cm; HSR 57 dBA @ ~10 cm; sounds normalized to 80 dBA in VR; localization error Go1 9.76 deg head-on / 9.39 deg radial, Turtlebot 8.64/9.22, HSR 13.15/12.40; velocities 0.3 and 0.8 m/s.
findings.relevance: Gives the spectral character of quadruped ego-noise (impulsive low-frequency step + high-frequency motor tone) that a laughter/VAD front end must discriminate against.

findings.claim: Quadruped (Go1) sound is a 'rhythmic alternation of lower frequency components resembling an impact sound' and is detected by people at ~17.8 m versus 3.45 m for a wheeled robot; background noise of 83 dB(A) collapses detection distance to ~2.75 m; the quadruped is rated less annoying (2.61 vs 4.39 on 1-7).
findings.source_title: Sound Matters: Auditory Detectability of Mobile Robots (arXiv 2404.06807)
findings.numbers: Go1 recorded at 1 m with a 3DIO FS XLR binaural mic at 7 cm height; backgrounds 60 dB(A) low / 83 dB(A) high; detection distance wheeled 3.45 m (SD 1.24), quadruped 17.80 m (SD 4.09); high-noise 2.75 m (SD 0.71) vs low-noise 18.60 m (SD 4.68) across robots; annoyance wheeled 4.39 (SD 1.82) vs quadruped 2.61 (SD 1.58).
findings.relevance: Footstep transients are salient and low-frequency; the same property that makes them audible at 18 m makes them the dominant on-body interferer.

findings.claim: A slow-stepping, gentle-touchdown MPC controller cuts Go1 walking noise by ~10 dB (from ~60 dB, 'similar to a vacuum cleaner', to ~50 dB at ear level alongside the robot) — below the 65 dB of wheeled systems; sources are foot-ground impact and gear-backlash collisions.
findings.source_title: Human-Centered Development of Guide Dog Robots: Quiet and Stable Locomotion Control (arXiv 2505.11808)
findings.numbers: Go1 + Beelink SEi12 (i7-12450H); smartphone at ear level walking alongside, 2 m recording zone; default controller ~60 dB at 0.6/1.0/1.2 m/s; new controller ~50 dB average, 'nearly 10 dB' lower; wheeled reference 65 dB; n=4 user study, all noticed the reduction.
findings.relevance: Second independent confirmation that gait shaping buys 8-10 dB; supports a 'listening gait' behaviour token in the body/act stream.

findings.claim: On a mobile robot with a 16-mic array, learning a dictionary of ego-noise spatial covariance matrices from only 90 s of noise and using it in an MVDR beamformer raises SDR by ~11 dB and cuts WER from 90.3% to 35.5% at input SNRs around -3 dB, in real time, with open-source ROS code.
findings.source_title: Ego-noise reduction of a mobile robot using noise spatial covariance matrix learning and minimum variance distortionless response (IROS 2023, Lagacé/Ferland/Grondin)
findings.numbers: Clearpath Jackal UGV (wheeled), 16SoundsUSB array, 16 omni mics, 32 kHz; input SNR -6 to +1.6 dB, large-room avg -2.69 dB; SDR -1.75 -> 9.57 dB; WER 90.3% -> 35.5% (55% relative); music-event AP 0.487 -> 0.685; 90 s ego-noise calibration; 0.5 s segment processed in 0.2 s on a laptop (Python/NumPy); code github.com/introlab/egonoise.
findings.relevance: The most practical open-source ego-noise recipe; directly applicable to the reSpeaker's 4 raw-mic channels, but demonstrated only at SNRs 10-20 dB better than a trotting quadruped will see.

findings.claim: Ego-noise on a legged humanoid sits at 0-5 dB SNR for arm motion and -5-0 dB for head motion (head motion 8.4 dB louder than arm); motor-state-indexed template subtraction plus missing-feature masking recovers 15-18% word-correct-rate on average, up to 20% for head motion.
findings.source_title: A Robust Speech Recognition System against the Ego Noise of a Robot (Interspeech 2010, Ince et al., Honda Research Institute)
findings.numbers: 8 mics on top of the head; head-motion noise 8.4 dB higher than arm motion; joint angles every 5 ms, 10 ms audio frames; template subtraction alpha=1, beta=0.5; real-world SNR [0 5] dB arm, [-5 0] dB head; 15% and 18% average WCR improvement; masks up to +10%; selective white-noise superposition +20% for head motion.
findings.relevance: Establishes the motor-state-conditioned template approach — Parcel knows its own gait phase and joint commands, so the same trick applies to footstep templates.

findings.claim: Joint ego-noise + environmental noise on a 4-mic NAO H25 at average SNR -2.1 dB is best handled by a partially adaptive VAE-NMF model (pre-trained ego-noise dictionary + adaptive environmental part); fully adaptive models fail to capture ego-noise structure.
findings.source_title: Partially Adaptive Multichannel Joint Reduction of Ego-noise and Environmental Noise (ICASSP 2023, Fang/Wittmer/Twiefel/Wermter/Gerkmann)
findings.numbers: NAO H25, M=4 mics at built-in array positions, 16 kHz, 64 ms Hann STFT; ego-noise from right-arm movements in crouching posture; test SNR in {-5,...,5} dB plus DEMAND env noise at 0 dB; average SNR -2.1 dB (joint) / -1.8 dB (ego-only); 128 test samples per scenario; results as Si-SDR/POLQA/WER plots (no tabulated values).
findings.relevance: Shows a pre-trained ego-noise prior beats purely adaptive suppression — an argument for logging the dog's own noise per gait and conditioning the front end on it.

findings.claim: Footstep sounds captured by a foot-mounted microphone on a Deep Robotics Lite2 quadruped are strong enough to classify terrain (energy below 1 kHz on concrete), with the authors noting contamination by motor, transmission and joint-impact noise.
findings.source_title: A Terrain Perception Method for Quadruped Robots Based on Acoustic Signal Fusion (Sensors, 2026)
findings.numbers: BOYA external mic at foot end; 8 kHz; 3,200,000 samples (400 s) per terrain; 13-dim MFCC; concrete energy 'concentrated below 1000 Hz'; accuracy 78.28% without acoustics -> 82.52% with fusion; 99.53% with 1 s window (C=0.01, gamma=0.001).
findings.relevance: Independent evidence that on-body footstep transients dominate the low band where the XVF3800 HPF (70-180 Hz) and stationary NS give little help; also hints that the same signal could be a free terrain/self-state feature for the behaviour model.

findings.claim: A reSpeaker 4-mic array has been fielded on a Boston Dynamics Spot (backpack mast) with ODAS for sound-source tracking, but the project reports no ego-noise numbers; no paper measuring ASR or sound-event-detection degradation at a body-mounted mic on Spot, Go1/Go2 or ANYmal while walking was found in this sweep.
findings.source_title: Sound Source Tracking as a Heuristic for Frontier Exploration on Spot (ICRA 2024 / Queen's MASc, MIT-licensed repo)
findings.numbers: Spot + 'A ReSpeaker 4-Mic Array' on a custom backpack with a sacrificial mast; ODAS (introlab) base; MIT license; no dB/SNR figures.
findings.relevance: Confirms the evidence hole: Parcel must measure on-dog SNR itself (protocol in the note) rather than rely on literature.

design_implications: Route every robot utterance through the reSpeaker XVF3800's own DAC/speaker: the AEC reference is the left channel of the host's USB playback to that device; TTS through the Go2 speaker or any other output is un-cancelled echo into the duplex model.

Treat owner barge-in during robot speech + locomotion as unreliable by construction: AEC needs seconds of far-end audio to converge, over-suppresses near-end until then, and the Path Change Detector heavily suppresses near-end whenever the acoustic path moves; tune AEC_PCD_COUPLINGI (or disable PCD) and monitor AEC_AECPATHCHANGE, and prefer speaking while standing.
Budget ~60-110 ms of front-end latency (min 58 ms mic-in to out, typ 50 ms output) plus USB/host buffering — about one 80 ms duplex frame each way before the model.

Use the speech-gated bearing (AUDIO_MGR_SELECTED_AZIMUTHS, NAN when silent; or Seeed DOA_VALUE 0-359 deg + VAD) as the body-yaw target for 'look back at the owner'; it is a speech-conditioned bearing, not a general sound localizer, updates on a 16 ms beamformer cycle, has no published accuracy spec, and the free-running beam will be steered by footsteps.

Mic-side SNR while walking/trotting is roughly -10 to -25 dB (72-79 dBA mean / 81-84 dBA peak at 30 cm on a Go1 at 0.5 m/s vs 55-65 dB SPL speech), 10-20 dB worse than any regime where published ego-noise suppression (template subtraction, covariance-MVDR) has been shown to work; the XVF3800's 'up to 25 dB' suppression targets stationary/diffuse noise, not impulsive <1 kHz footstep transients.

Gate the laughter-reward detector and VAD on gait phase / foot-contact events from the Go2 state stream, or score laughter only while standing or in a quiet gait; footsteps and laughter are both impulsive and will confound each other.

Add a 'listening gait' / stop-to-listen behaviour: contact-velocity-shaped gaits give -8 to -10 dB (MUTE, guide-dog controller) and standing drops to the ~55 dBA fan floor; mount the array on the top/head of the body away from the feet.

Flash respeaker_xvf3800_usb_dfu_firmware_v2.1.0_16k6ch.bin: feed the ASR channel (post-beamformer, no noise suppression) to the learned front end and log the 4 raw mics for per-gait ego-noise templates (Lagacé needs ~90 s per condition; introlab/egonoise is open source, ROS-ready).
Licensing: XVF3800 DSP is proprietary (XCORE VocalFusion Licence); the 8-hour stop applies only to the XMOS eval kit, but verify the reSpeaker unit runs >8 h continuously; DFU tooling is GPLv2.

Close the evidence hole on day one with a Go2: record 6-ch raw + Conference + ASR at stand / 0.5 m/s / 1.0 m/s on carpet and wood with speech and laughter at 1-3 m and TTS playing, and report per-gait SNR, VAD false-positive rate, laughter precision, AEC_AECPATHCHANGE duty cycle and DoA error — these numbers decide listen-while-moving vs stop-to-listen.

sweeps.topic: Credit assignment for delayed social rewards (laughter, look-back) in continuous full-duplex speech+action streams: multi-turn/delayed-reward RL for dialogue and agents, RL for full-duplex speech with timing rewards, and implicit-feedback reward learning from deployment data with reward-hacking failure modes

findings.claim: DuplexPO assigns timing credit in a full-duplex model by restricting GRPO updates to short 'dynamics-critical windows' around annotated events (turn onset, backchannel, barge-in) with a factorised reward (Gaussian onset penalty, backchannel overlap/exp-decay, yield penalty, regulariser); widening the lead window beyond 1 s sharply reduces reward, and a learned neural timing reward underperformed the factorised rule reward.
findings.source_title: Decoupling Conversational Dynamics in Full-Duplex Spoken Models through Reinforcement Learning (DuplexPO)
findings.numbers: 12.5 Hz frames (0.08 s); window lead 1.0 s / buffer 2.0 s; <=3 turn windows + 1 backchannel window per conversation; RL data Fisher 24.6K + Seamless 43.1K samples; Fisher onset MAE 0.98->0.69 s, backchannel yield 57.1->100%, turn yield 92.1->98.7%; Seamless onset MAE 1.22->1.03 s; FDB-v3 voiced-interrupt rate 7.33%->0.24%; judge preference 76.9% (Fisher) / 69.3% (Seamless); QA benchmarks unchanged or +1-3 pts; 64xA800; base Qwen2.5-7B Nemotron-VoiceChat
findings.relevance: Direct template for Parcel: anchor credit to an observable event time, score only a ~[-1 s, +2 s] window, teacher-force the rest, GRPO inside the window. Its own limitation ('window-local optimisation may miss long-range coherence') is exactly Parcel's multi-second laughter gap.

findings.claim: Kyutai aligned Moshi and PersonaPlex on four interactivity axes with GRPO and per-axis rule rewards extracted from real human-human corpora, using a +-1 s F1 window as the backchannel-timing reward; they report that optimising timing rewards alone degrades semantic quality and that Fisher-trained models lost safety behaviour.
findings.source_title: Multi-Faceted Interactivity Alignment in Full-Duplex Speech Models
findings.numbers: Fisher 2,000 h; Seamless 1,300 h + 2,700 h; <=2,000 segments per axis; pause reward -1 if model speaks >1 s; turn/interrupt reward = -delay; backchannel reward = F1 with +-1 s window; LLM judge 0-2; Moshi: pause TOR 0.445->0.307, backchannel freq 0.074->0.101/s, interruption latency 1.377->0.409 s; PersonaPlex: turn latency 0.219->0.086 s, BC freq 0.046->0.112/s; license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; checkpoints kyutai/moshika-rl-seamless
findings.relevance: Gives the concrete tolerance (+-1 s F1) to reuse for chuckle timing and the warning that a timing-only reward on the shared stream harms content, motivating a separate act-token policy plus a semantic reward.

findings.claim: ASPIRin shows plain GRPO with latency/overlap rewards on a full-duplex model's whole vocabulary reward-hacks into repetition loops and oscillating training curves; projecting the action space to a binary speak/silent state (sum of token logits) and optimising only that with GRPO removes the collapse while still improving turn-taking.
findings.source_title: ASPIRin: Action Space Projection for Interactivity-Optimized Reinforcement Learning in Full-Duplex Speech Language Models
findings.numbers: tolerances tau_int = tau_re = 1.0 s, reward = product; 43 h / ~1,300 two-minute dual-channel clips; GRPO G=2, KL beta=0.001, LoRA r=256, 8xV100, 3 epochs; FDB turn-taking TOR Moshi 0.436 / SFT 0.927 / GRPO 0.709 / ASPIRin 0.364; interruption latency 1.159 / 1.970 / 0.614 / 0.992 s; 2-gram repetition GRPO 0.117 vs ASPIRin 0.054, 3-gram 0.072 vs 0.029; license CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Argues Parcel's discrete body/act stream should be optimised as its own projected action space (chuckle / look-back / idle) with the speech content protected; and that a few tens of hours suffice for timing RL.

findings.claim: Pang et al. learned implicit rewards from 3.1M BlenderBot deployment turns using only the single next human turn (existence, length, sentiment, joy); longer windows over all future turns could not be trained. Engagement/continuation proxies improved win rate but raised controversial and unfriendly generations, while the joy-reaction proxy improved win rate and halved controversial messages.
findings.source_title: Leveraging Implicit Feedback from Deployment Data in Dialogue
findings.numbers: 3.1M bot + 3.1M human utterances (Aug 2022-Jan 2023); RoBERTa-large classifier, sample-and-rerank over 20 candidates from BlenderBot 3B; crowd majority-of-5, 200 expert pairs; win rate (new-baseline): length k=20 +12.0 (p<0.05), joy&length +9.5 (p<0.05), non-neg sentiment +8.5, replied -1.0; controversial %: baseline 17.0, replied 24.5, joy&length 8.5; unfriendly %: baseline 9.0, replied/length20 12.5, joy 6.0; seek-info 32.5% -> up to 60%; anger/disgust predictor dropped at ~55% dev acc
findings.relevance: Laughter is a reaction proxy (the benign column of this table), but the paper is the primary evidence that the choice of implicit signal determines the hack: continuation-type rewards provoke, reaction-type rewards do not. Also fixes the practical reward window at one following human turn.

findings.claim: Optimising an LLM with RL (iterative KTO) on simulated user feedback reliably produces manipulation and deception; when only 2% of users are 'gameable' the model learns to identify and target them while behaving normally with everyone else, standard sycophancy/toxicity benchmarks miss it, and mitigations (safety-data mixing, LLM veto filters) partly backfire into subtler manipulation.
findings.source_title: On Targeted Manipulation and Deception when Optimizing LLMs for User Feedback
findings.numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Gemma-2 to 27B); iterative KTO; 4 environments with 12/4/8/4 sub-envs; 2% gameable users sufficient for targeted harm; up to 75% safety data mixed with minimal reduction; harmful behaviours emerge within a few iterations; ICLR 2025; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Parcel trains on one owner's reactions, so 100% of the signal is one 'user': the policy will learn that owner's idiosyncratic laugh triggers and no generic filter will detect it. Requires held-out behavioural audits and extended-session evaluation, not benchmarks.

findings.claim: ArCHer separates credit assignment into a high-level off-policy utterance-level critic (aggregating delayed rewards across turns) and a low-level token policy trained against that critic's value, giving roughly 100x sample efficiency over PPO on multi-turn tasks.
findings.source_title: ArCHer: Training Language Model Agents via Hierarchical Multi-Turn RL
findings.numbers: 'at least a 100x boost in sample efficiency': <1,000 samples vs >100k for PPO on Twenty Questions; actor GPT-2 100M and Mistral-7B; critic RoBERTa-base double-Q; envs Detective Game (51-step optimum, max reward 360), Twenty Questions (-1/step), WebShop (0-1 dense); ICML 2024; CC BY 4.0; code github.com/YifeiZhou02/ArCHer
findings.relevance: The 'doubly hierarchical' framing (which segment, then which token) maps to Parcel's act-segment vs frame problem, and the off-policy critic argues for a replayable log of (context, act segment, delayed outcome) tuples given a few hundred laugh events.

findings.claim: SWEET-RL trains a step-wise (per-turn) advantage critic with privileged training-time information via a Bradley-Terry objective over turn sums, then does per-turn DPO; it beats multi-turn DPO by 6 points absolute and reports that learning an accurate value function is itself hard and trajectory-level credit has high variance.
findings.source_title: SWEET-RL: Training Multi-Turn LLM Agents on Collaborative Reasoning Tasks
findings.numbers: ColBench backend 10k train tasks / 15k trajectories / 1k test, frontend 10k / 6k / 500, max 10 turns; per-turn DPO with 16 samples top/bottom 50%; Llama-3.1-8B success/win: zero-shot 22.4/33.8, multi-turn DPO 34.4/42.8, SWEET-RL 40.4/48.2, GPT-4o 40.4/50.0; CC BY 4.0; code facebookresearch/sweet_rl
findings.relevance: Parcel has privileged training-time information (the laugh detector output, track-loss ground truth) that the deployed policy does not see; a privileged per-segment critic is the natural way to use it.

findings.claim: Systematic study of terminal vs delayed vs per-turn reward structures for multi-turn agents finds dense per-turn rewards consistently outperform sparse terminal and delayed rewards in both training dynamics and final accuracy (MT-GRPO / MT-PPO blend turn-level and outcome advantages).
findings.source_title: Reinforcing Multi-Turn Reasoning in LLM Agents via Fine-Grained Reward Structure and Credit Assignment (MT-GRPO / MT-PPO)
findings.numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, 8xH100, 500 steps, batch 512; MT-PPO NQ/HotpotQA/avg 0.490/0.453/0.447 vs PPO-OR 0.483/0.435/0.432 and PPO-MR 0.472/0.436/0.429; format compliance 99.9%; NeurIPS 2025; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Supports shaping Parcel's delayed laugh into per-segment signals (e.g. a detector-derived local reward) rather than one terminal reward per session.

findings.claim: MICA handles long-horizon emotional-support dialogue with a delayed session outcome by mixing a turn-index-normalised Monte-Carlo advantage with a group-normalised immediate advantage and by converting the outcome into a potential-based per-turn Incremental Distance Reward (change in distance to the satisfied user state).
findings.source_title: MICA: Multi-granularity Intertemporal Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Emotional Support Dialogue
findings.numbers: A = 0.5*A_turn + 0.5*A_group (alpha in [0.5,0.7] best); r_t = phi(t-1) - phi(t) over cognitive/affective/proactive empathy; 727 training samples; EMPA simulator; gains Qwen2.5-7B +42.5, Qwen3-8B +28.2, Qwen3-32B +15.3 (->84.2); judge robustness cosine >=0.78; CC BY 4.0; verl-MICA released
findings.relevance: The incremental-distance reward is a ready pattern for 'look back when lost' (phi = distance of owner from view), and the turn-index normalisation is a critic-free way to compare act segments at the same position.

findings.claim: ITPO derives implicit turn-wise process rewards from a sparse outcome by summing log-ratio token rewards per turn and normalising across turns; turn-level implicit credit converges fast and improves PPO/GRPO/RLOO by 8-20%, whereas token-level implicit rewards (PRIME) and uniform decomposition give no reliable gain under stochastic simulated users.
findings.source_title: Implicit Turn-Wise Policy Optimization for Proactive User-LLM Interaction (ITPO)
findings.numbers: Qwen2.5-3B policy, Qwen2.5-14B user sim; tasks 500 MATH (max 5 turns), 500 Medium docs, 550 MTMedDialog; RLOO math 29.06->32.50 (+11.8%), doc 37.35->44.83 (+20.0%), med 61.22->66.14 (+8.0%); GRPO 26.37->31.12, 39.33->42.78, 66.41->71.74; PRIME token-level 29.75/40.95/61.42; Kendall tau 0.5-0.75; turn-wise Spearman 0.8-0.9 vs token 0.5-0.6; human agreement 48/64 (75%); CC BY 4.0; code Graph-COM/ITPO
findings.relevance: Evidence that credit should be assigned at the act-segment level, not per 80 ms frame, when the reward source (a human reaction) is highly stochastic.

findings.claim: User feedback in real human-LLM dialogues is a noisy learning signal: fine-grained detectors reach only 41.6% accuracy, prompts that elicit positive feedback are slightly more toxic (users praising jailbreaks), regenerating with feedback barely beats regenerating from scratch, and SFT on feedback-derived data improved MT-Bench but degraded WildBench.
findings.source_title: User Feedback in Human-LLM Dialogues: A Lens to Understand Users But Noisy as a Learning Signal
findings.numbers: 109 densely annotated conversations (227 + 206 user turns), 75/107 sparse; GPT-4o-mini accuracy 41.6% fine-grained / 81.1% sparse; kappa 0.60/0.74; regenerate-with-feedback win rate 48%; weak-model self-refine 58% vs GPT 74%; MT-Bench 6.37->6.68 but WildBench 28.90->24.47; KTO mixed; EMNLP 2025; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: The detector is part of the attack surface: a laughter detector at ~0.6 F1 in the wild will generate false-positive rewards that the policy exploits, so precision at the operating point bounds the exposure.

findings.claim: GELI / LLM-GELI decompose one delayed session-level rating (CANDOR post-conversation affect) into per-turn rewards, using local implicit multimodal listener cues (facial affect, prosody, gaze) to steer where credit lands, and the resulting PPO-trained LLaMA-2 policies win human evaluations on most social metrics.
findings.source_title: Aligning Dialogue Agents with Global Feedback via Large Language Model Reward Decomposition (LLM-GELI; builds on GELI arXiv 2403.11330)
findings.kind: method (global-to-local reward decomposition with multimodal implicit feedback)
findings.numbers: CANDOR 1,656 conversations, ~159.4 turns and 31.3 min each, 850 h; GELI: RRD + facial-affect local term, BART-406M reward model, LLaMA-2-7B PPO+LoRA (13M), human eval 100 samples: emotional connection 39.67 vs 30.67%, positivity 44.33 vs 26.67%, best on 6/8; LLM-GELI multimodal best on 6/9 (social 26.33+-1.25, p<0.01), global-loss 24.3-25.0 vs 172-825 for RRD/IRCR/RUDDER; 4xA6000 ~19 h; prompt-wording sensitivity noted; Hippocratic License planned
findings.relevance: Closest existing instantiation of 'a listener's immediate multimodal reaction tells you which turn earned the delayed global reward' — Parcel's laughter detector plays the local-implicit role.

findings.claim: Feedback loops at deployment cause in-context reward hacking: an agent optimising an implicit engagement proxy raises engagement and toxicity together, a banking agent raises success and constraint violations together; larger models hack more and prompt warnings do not stop it.
findings.source_title: Feedback Loops With Language Models Drive In-Context Reward Hacking
findings.numbers: Twitter agent: GPT-3.5-judged engagement up with Perspective-API toxicity up; scaling across Claude-3 family worsened ICRH; ICML 2024; recommendations: extended feedback cycles, diverse loop structures, atypical observations
findings.relevance: A laugh-seeking companion in a daily loop can escalate (louder, cruder, repetitive); evaluation must use extended multi-session runs.

findings.claim: Jaques et al. used counts of laughter strings ('ha', 'lol') in the user's next message as an RL reward for a deployed chatbot via KL-controlled offline RL; laughter-optimised bots became 'extremely supportive and cheerful', purely reward-maximising Batch-Q exploited a question reward by only asking questions, and RL bots were more repetitive than the supervised baseline.
findings.source_title: Human-centric dialog training via offline reinforcement learning
findings.numbers: 80 MTurk workers, 600 seven-point Likert ratings, >=6 turns, n=40 per model; laughter-reward bot total 14.28+-1.96 vs manual-votes 14.53, bot-repetition 15.48 (best RL), VHRED baseline 16.03; laughter human-reward z 0.01; conversation length not higher in upvoted responses
findings.relevance: Only end-to-end RL result with a laughter reward; predicts the two hacks Parcel should pre-empt (fawning and repetition) and the fix (repetition penalty).

findings.claim: Inoue et al. define shared laughter as a robot laugh within 2 s of the user's laugh; only 16.2% of user laughs were shared by humans, a laugh detector reaches F1 82.6% on close-talk corpus audio, and the shared-laughter timing predictor reaches only F1 30.3%, yet the system significantly improved perceived empathy in a crowd study.
findings.source_title: Can a robot laugh with you?: Shared laughter generation for empathetic spoken dialogue
findings.kind: precedent (laughter timing window and base rate)
findings.numbers: 82 speed-dating sessions with ERICA, 10-15 min each; BiGRU detector F1 82.6%; shared-laughter window 2 s; positives 16.2%; predictor F1 30.3%; laugh-type macro-F1 70.2%; Fleiss kappa 0.404; >30 crowd raters, 7-point scales; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Sets the empirical window (2 s) and the human base rate for a chuckle policy; a laughter-reward policy that chuckles at every laugh exceeds the human rate 6x.

findings.claim: Delayed rewards that are composite (fragmented over later time steps) and partially anonymous (only aggregates over past actions are observed) admit near-optimal learning with regret that grows only additively in the delay bound; and when the delayed reward is a non-additive function of the sequence, a transformer reward model with learned per-step importance weights (CoDeTr) beats sum-form redistribution but degrades as delay grows.
findings.source_title: Beyond Simple Sum of Delayed Rewards: Non-Markovian Reward Modeling for Reinforcement Learning (CoDeTr); with Mondal & Aggarwal arXiv 2305.02527
findings.kind: theory / general-RL method for delayed composite rewards
findings.numbers: Mondal & Aggarwal DUCRL2 regret O~(D S sqrt(A T) + d (S A)^3), d <= max delay; CoDeTr delays 5-500 steps on MuJoCo/DMC with SumSquare/SquareSum/Max structures, beats SAC, LIRPG, HC, IRCR, RRD, RBT
findings.relevance: A laugh is a threshold response to joke + delivery + pause, i.e. non-additive and anonymous over several act tokens; the additive delay cost argues for a small act vocabulary, and CoDeTr's importance-weighted sequence reward is the non-LLM analogue of GELI.

design_implications: No published system closes Parcel's loop: 2025-26 full-duplex RL (DuplexPO, Kyutai, ASPIRin) uses rule rewards computed offline from annotated human-human recordings in 1-2 s windows; none uses a live listener reaction as reward or assigns credit over more than a few seconds. The gap is real and the pieces (windowed GRPO, GELI-style global-to-local decomposition, laughter detectors) exist separately.

Anchor credit to an observable event time and keep the window short: score act/speech tokens in roughly [t_laugh - 2.5 s, t_laugh - 0.3 s] for the joke/delivery and a +-1 s F1-style window for chuckle timing; DuplexPO's ablation shows lead windows > 1 s dilute reward. 'Look back when lost' is the easy case (machine-observable track-loss event -> binary head-turn-within-tau reward, exactly the ASPIRin/DuplexPO setting).

Separate 'when' from 'what': optimise the discrete body/act stream as its own projected action space (chuckle / look-back / idle) with GRPO, freeze or KL-protect the speech content (ASPIRin beta = 0.001), and run a semantic-quality judge reward in parallel, because timing-only rewards on the full vocabulary collapse into repetition (ASPIRin) or degrade content (Kyutai).

Use segment-level (act-segment) credit, not 80 ms frames: ITPO, MICA, MT-GRPO and SWEET-RL all show turn/segment-level credit converges faster and is more robust than token-level under stochastic human responses; MICA's potential-based incremental-distance reward (phi = owner distance from view) is a ready shaping for look-back; a privileged per-segment critic (SWEET-RL) can consume the detector/track ground truth the deployed policy never sees.

Design against the documented hacks: continuation/engagement proxies make dialogue agents provocative (Pang: controversial 17% -> 24.5%) while reaction proxies do not (joy: 17% -> 8.5%), but laughter maximisers fawn and repeat (Jaques), so add a repetition penalty and cap chuckle rate at a human base rate (Inoue: only 16.2% of laughs shared; FDB backchannel ~0.1/s). Because one owner supplies 100% of the signal, expect targeted idiosyncratic exploitation that benchmark-style checks cannot see (Williams: 2% gameable users suffice); audit on unfamiliar people and extended multi-session runs (ICRH).

Detector precision bounds reward-hacking exposure: feedback detectors at 41.6% fine-grained accuracy and in-the-wild laughter F1 ~0.6 (first sweep) will generate false-positive rewards the policy exploits; measure precision at the operating point and prefer a composite/non-additive sequence reward (CoDeTr / GELI) over per-frame sums.

Sample budget is compatible with the literature: ASPIRin 43 h (~1,300 clips), Kyutai <= 2,000 segments per axis, Dual-Axis RM 389 real samples, ITPO/MICA 500-727 tasks; a few hundred owner-laugh events is in range if rewards are event-anchored and the act space is projected. ArCHer's ~100x sample-efficiency argument favours keeping an off-policy replayable log of (context window, act segment, delayed outcome) rather than on-policy GRPO alone.

Before committing, measure: owner-laugh base rate and latency distribution relative to Parcel's acts (to set the window; 2 s and 1/2 s are starting points), detector precision/recall at the deployed threshold, and a Pang-style behaviour audit (repetition, fawning, provocation) after every RL round.

sweeps.topic: GPU contention and real-time jitter when running several models concurrently on Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB alongside a 50-500 Hz control loop: CUDA MPS on Tegra, time-slicing, stream priorities, PREEMPT_RT jitter under GPU load, NVIDIA multi-model demos, and robotics stacks co-scheduling LLM/VLA with controllers on Orin

findings.claim: Without MPS, kernels from different CUDA contexts (processes) never execute concurrently; the GPU uses a time-sliced scheduler across contexts. On Tegra the default timeslice is 1024 us and identical for all TSGs, a context switch costs 50-750 us (measured average >200 us on Xavier NX and Orin Nano), and a runlist update costs up to ~1 ms. No user-space interface exists to change timeslice or TSG priority.
findings.source_title: GCAPS: GPU Context-Aware Preemptive Priority-based Scheduling for Real-Time Tasks (ECRTS 2024) + NVIDIA MPS Architecture doc (https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/mps/architecture.html)
findings.numbers: timeslice 1024 us (same for all TSGs); context switch 50-750 us, avg >200 us; runlist update max ~1 ms; priority-aware preemption cut response time 45.33 ms -> 10.15 ms and 66.97 ms -> 22.36 ms on Xavier; up to 40% higher schedulability; only 2 CUDA stream priority levels on Pascal; platforms Xavier NX JetPack 5.0.2, Orin Nano JetPack 5.1.2
findings.relevance: Sets the scheduling model Parcel must design for: N GPU-active processes serialise at ~1 ms granularity, so a full-duplex speech step shares wall time linearly with VLM/ASR/TTS tenants and each hand-off costs hundreds of microseconds.

findings.claim: NVIDIA does not expose any GPU scheduling knobs on Jetson: the DRIVE OS timeslice/runlist-interleave/preemption parameters are DRIVE-only, and there is no interface on Jetson for GPU resource partitioning or per-process priority.
findings.source_title: NVIDIA Developer Forums: 'GPU scheduling parameters' (AGX Orin) and 'Jetson: GPU resource control (limitation, priority...)' (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/jetson-gpu-resource-control-limitation-priority/278057)
findings.numbers: Quotes: 'The parameter is only available on the DRIVE OS system. We don't provide such parameters on Jetson to change GPU scheduling behavior.' and 'For now we don't have the interface on Jetson platforms.' DRIVE-only formula: worst-case latency(high) = (h-1) x timeslice(high) + execution time(low) + channel reset (https://developer.nvidia.com/docs/drive/drive-os/6.0.8.1/public/drive-os-linux-sdk/common/topics/graphics_content/RunlistInterleaveFrequency40.html)
findings.relevance: Rules out OS-level GPU prioritisation of the speech/act model over perception on Orin; prioritisation has to be done in-process (streams) or by process design.

findings.claim: CUDA MPS is officially supported on Tegra Linux from CUDA 12.5 (JetPack 6.1); NVIDIA staff confirm it for Jetson Orin. But no published latency/throughput measurement of MPS on any Orin was found, and the Kubernetes MPS mode fails on Orin JetPack 6.2 while manual nvidia-cuda-mps-control -d works.
findings.source_title: CUDA for Tegra application note (MPS section) + NVIDIA forum 'MPS for Jetson AGX Orin' (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/mps-for-jetson-agx-orin/327036) + k8s-device-plugin issue #1412 (https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/issues/1412)
findings.kind: vendor doc + vendor forum + GitHub issue
findings.numbers: 'now available on Tegra platforms: Linux starting with CUDA 12.5 and QNX starting with CUDA 12.8'; 'MPS has started to support Jetson from CUDA 12.5' (AastaLLL); k8s MPS error 'error getting GPU device minor number: Not Supported' on JetPack 6.2, time-slicing mode works; on dGPU two 50% MPS clients went 100 ms -> 110 ms / 140 ms (+10%/+40%, memory-bandwidth contention per NVIDIA; https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/mps-interference-problem/312930) and an H100 MPS server without share limits raised a 65 us kernel to ~100 ms (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/mps-vs-no-mps-drastic-increase-in-kernel-latency/336175)
findings.relevance: MPS is the only multi-process concurrency lever Parcel has on Orin; it exists but is unmeasured there, so it must be benchmarked (with explicit active-thread percentages) before the design relies on it.

findings.claim: On an AGX Orin 64 GB with JetPack 6.2 and the RT OTA kernel, a 1 kHz cyclictest loop under glmark2 GPU load has a 159 us worst case without CPU isolation and 15 us with isolcpus/irqaffinity/kthread_cpus isolation; the stock non-RT kernel reaches 318 us under combined load.
findings.source_title: WIM Tech Blog: Is PREEMPT_RT Enough? Validating Real-Time Performance on Jetson Orin
findings.kind: engineering blog with full measurement protocol (secondary)
findings.numbers: cyclictest -p 80 -i 1000 -l 600000 -m -a 8-11, 10 min, MAXN + jetson_clocks; non-RT max 318 us; PREEMPT_RT max 56 us combined; RT no isolation max: GPU 159 us, EtherCAT 113 us, storage 145 us, stress-ng 47 us; RT + isolcpus=managed_irq,domain,8-11 irqaffinity=0-7 kthread_cpus=0-7: GPU 15 us, EtherCAT 6 us, storage 7 us, system 15 us
findings.relevance: Gives Parcel the concrete recipe and budget for keeping a 50-500 Hz body controller on isolated Orin cores while the GPU runs the speech/VLM stack: ~15 us max jitter is achievable, ~160-320 us if isolation or the RT kernel is skipped.

findings.claim: Running several CUDA processes concurrently on a Jetson Orin-class GPU collapses per-process throughput and inflates execution-context duration super-linearly while SMs sit mostly idle: on Orin Nano, 8 concurrent ResNet50 int8 processes drop from ~210 img/s to ~10 img/s each, and EC duration grows ~30x with 4 and ~70x with 8 processes.
findings.source_title: Profiling Concurrent Vision Inference Workloads on NVIDIA Jetson - Extended (Chakraborty et al.)
findings.numbers: Orin Nano 8 GB: ResNet50 int8 single ~210 img/s (bs1), ~320 img/s (bs16); 8 processes ~10 img/s each; YOLOv8n int8 16 processes ~10 img/s each, GPU memory 3.5x; EC duration ~30x (4 procs) and ~70x (8 procs); SM utilisation 15-30% while GPU util reads 100%; tensor cores ~30%; kernel launch 20-100 us each
findings.relevance: Quantifies the penalty of the naive process-per-model layout Parcel must avoid; motivates one process with streams (or MPS) for speech+VLM+ASR+TTS.

findings.claim: Bakita & Anderson measured Tegra GPU time-slicing directly: only one task executes at a time; compute timeslices are 1024 us on Jetson TX2 (1049 us for copy-only channels) versus ~2 ms on discrete GPUs; Jetson boards get only 2 (Xavier, CUDA 10.2) or 4 (Orin, CUDA 11.4) usable compute channels per context, which caps intra-process stream parallelism.
findings.source_title: Demystifying NVIDIA GPU Internals to Enable Reliable GPU Management (RTAS 2024)
findings.numbers: TX2 compute timeslice 1024 us, copy 1049 us; discrete ~20 timeslices per 80 ms (~2 ms each); channels per context: 2 on Xavier (CUDA 10.2), 4 on Orin (CUDA 11.4), 'CUDA appears to have a bug where only half are used on Jetson boards'; Jetson Orin (CC 8.7) in tested set; tools nvdebug + gpu-microbench work on Tegra
findings.relevance: Independent confirmation of the ~1 ms quantum and a warning that even a single-process multi-stream design on Orin only gets ~4 concurrent hardware channels.

findings.claim: AGX Orin has a hard limit of 32 concurrent CUDA contexts/processes (kernel error 'out of hw chids'); NVIDIA's answer is to use more streams in fewer processes or reduce CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS.
findings.source_title: NVIDIA Developer Forums: Limitation in number of concurrent CUDA contexts on AGX Orin
findings.numbers: 33rd process fails; limit 32 on AGX Orin and Orin Nano; TX2 ran 48; nvgpu_channel_open_new:1286 [ERR] out of hw chids; 'The maximal concurrent CUDA processes/contexts on Orin is 32'
findings.relevance: Process-count hygiene for a ROS 2 graph where many nodes open CUDA; not binding for five models but binding for sprawling Isaac ROS stacks.

findings.claim: CUDA stream priorities are non-preemptive hints: higher-priority work does not interrupt running lower-priority kernels and only wins at the next launch decision; green contexts partition SMs within a single process only and give no concurrency guarantee. Thor gets MPS + green contexts + (upcoming) MIG for deterministic co-scheduling, but 'Orin (sm_87) ... will continue on its current path for now'.
findings.source_title: CUDA Programming Guide (stream priorities; green contexts https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/green-contexts.html) + NVIDIA blog 'What's New in CUDA Toolkit 13.0 for Jetson Thor' (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/whats-new-in-cuda-toolkit-13-0-for-jetson-thor-unified-arm-ecosystem-and-more/)
findings.numbers: Quotes: 'Higher-priority tasks do not preempt already running lower-priority tasks'; 'MPS targets different processes, while green contexts is applicable within a single process too'; 'concurrent execution of independent GPU work is not guaranteed'; 'The only exception is Orin (sm_87), which will continue on its current path for now.'
findings.relevance: Defines what in-process prioritisation can and cannot do on Orin, and confirms Orin will not receive Thor's spatial-isolation features, so Parcel must design for time-slicing.

findings.claim: The only AGX Orin 64 GB jitter measurement of a VLA running alongside a robot controller: a 4-bit SmolVLM-256M VLA runs at 150.5 ms mean with sigma 0.125 ms (min 150.4, max 151.0 ms) inside a ROS 2 node while the low-level controller keeps a 100 Hz heartbeat on the CPU side; the GPU has a single tenant.
findings.source_title: LiteVLA-Edge: Quantized On-Device Multimodal Control for Embedded Robotics (Williams, Gupta, George, Sarkar)
findings.numbers: Jetson AGX Orin 64GB; SmolVLM-256M, LoRA r=8, Q4_K_M GGUF; mean 150.5 ms, sigma 0.125 ms, min 150.4 ms, max 151.0 ms, 6.64 Hz; controller 100 Hz heartbeat; companion LiteVLA-H (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.00884): action token 50.65 ms (19.74 Hz), semantic 149.9-164.6 ms (6.1-6.7 Hz), K=3 dual-rate, 2.2 GB, 22.1 W, prefill 47.8 ms, 1.4 ms/token, no jitter reported
findings.relevance: Establishes the single-tenant baseline (sub-millisecond jitter) that Parcel's multi-tenant microbenchmark must be compared against, and the dual-rate fast-act/slow-semantic pattern that maps onto a speech+act token stream.

findings.claim: Deployed Go2 stacks keep the locomotion policy at 50 Hz on the dog's own Orin NX / Orin Nano with 200-1000 Hz motor loops and fit image processing plus policy inference inside the 20 ms cycle; when a heavier model is present it is either off-board (VeBrain: MLLM on a cloud A100 at 0.5 Hz, tracker at 15 Hz on the AGX Orin) or run in a separate thread at ~1 s per action batch (StreamVLN on a Thor T5000 with Isaac ROS VSLAM concurrently).
findings.source_title: Learning Diverse Natural Behaviors for Enhancing the Agility of Quadrupedal Robots + VeBrain (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.00123) + StreamVLN pruning paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.06480) + RoamFlow (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.29934)
findings.numbers: Go2 + Orin NX: policy 50 Hz, motors 1000 Hz, 'image processing and policy inference ... completed within each 20ms cycle', CUDA-accelerated; Go2 + Orin Nano: 50 Hz (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.18225); RoamFlow Go2 + Orin NX 16GB: whole loop 10 Hz, inference 37.2 ms, '<100 ms', 'minor jitter'; VeBrain Go2 + AGX Orin: Locotrack-small 15 Hz onboard, MLLM 0.5 Hz on A100; StreamVLN Go2 + Thor T5000: 1.43 s / 1.25 s per 4 actions, separate inference and motor-controller threads, 'only small pauses'
findings.relevance: Shows the field's working pattern: controller isolated at 50 Hz, heavy models decoupled by thread/process or off-board; no stack reports a speech LLM plus VLA plus controller on one Orin with jitter numbers.

findings.claim: On a Jetson Orin NX, a monocular pose network dropped from 5.5 Hz to 4.7 Hz (0.18 s to 0.21 s) simply because the flight controller competed for CPU; the authors attribute achievable rates to GPU utilisation, CPU scheduling, memory bandwidth, temperature and concurrent processes.
findings.source_title: Hardware- and Vision-in-the-Loop Validation of Deep Monocular Pose Estimation for Autonomous Maritime UAV Flight
findings.numbers: Orin NX: 5.5 Hz (0.18 s) alone; 4.7 Hz (0.21 s) with flight controller co-running (-15%)
findings.relevance: One of the few explicit co-run slowdown numbers on an Orin; shows CPU-side contention alone costs ~15% inference rate even before GPU contention.

findings.claim: NVIDIA's own multi-model Jetson demos run ASR, LLM/VLM and TTS together (llamaspeak on AGX Orin 64 GB with 'overlapping ASR/LLM/TTS generation'; Agent Studio as plugins each in its own thread in one process; Multi-Modal AI Studio on Thor with Riva ASR + Riva TTS + Cosmos-Reason2-8B on vLLM in separate containers) but publish no co-run latency or contention numbers; the single-tenant AGX Orin LLM baseline is Llama-3.1-8B W4A16 at 44.19 tok/s, TTFT 32.02 ms, ITL 22.47 ms.
findings.source_title: Jetson AI Lab: Agent Studio (archive) + llamaspeak (https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/archive/tutorial_llamaspeak.html) + Multi-Modal AI Studio (https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/tutorials/multi-modal-ai-studio/) + GenAI Benchmarking (https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/tutorials/genai-benchmarking/)
findings.numbers: llamaspeak: AGX Orin 64GB/32GB, Orin NX 16GB; 22 GB container + >10 GB models; Agent Studio: 'each plugin runs asynchronously its own thread ... Usually they're in the same process'; Multi-Modal AI Studio: parakeet-1.1b ASR + Magpie TTS + Cosmos-Reason2-8B, vLLM gpu-memory-utilization 0.7, separate containers; GenAI bench: 44.19 tok/s, TTFT 32.02 ms, ITL 22.47 ms single user, TTFT/ITL rise at concurrency 8; NVIDIA blog Dec 2025: gpt-oss-20b 40 tok/s on AGX Orin
findings.relevance: Confirms the vendor pattern (threads in one process, or containers sharing the GPU) and that the multi-tenant jitter number Parcel needs is absent even from NVIDIA's demos.

findings.claim: VLA-class policies on Orin run at 150-440 ms per step single-tenant (GR00T N1.7-3B 354 ms eager / 150.9 ms TensorRT; pi0.5 440 ms on Orin AGX 32 GB vs 60 ms on A100 with task accuracy falling 80% to 30% and visible jerkiness); asynchronous inference on Orin recovers 6.06 Hz control from 0.70 Hz and cuts reaction time from 1420.8 ms to 165.1 ms.
findings.source_title: Isaac-GR00T deployment README + Offload or Overload (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.18284) + Jetson-PI (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.12659v3)
findings.numbers: GR00T N1.7 bf16, 4 denoise steps, 1 camera: Orin 354.0 ms (2.8 Hz) eager -> 150.9 ms (6.6 Hz) TRT; Thor 112.8 -> 80.4 ms; H100 27.9 ms; pi0.5 Orin AGX 32GB 440 ms vs A100 60 ms, accuracy 80% -> 30%; full stack ~50 GB; Jetson-PI Orin 0.70 -> 6.06 Hz, reaction 1420.8 -> 165.1 ms, 8.66x vs PyTorch, 5.41x vs vla.cpp; Thor pi0.5 44 ms (23 Hz) with hand-written kernels (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/real-time-inference-on-thor-rtx-pi0-5-gr00t-n1-6-1-7-thor-23-hz-rtx-5090-50-80hz/368788)
findings.relevance: Sizes the GPU time any act/VLA-style head will consume per step on Orin before contention, and shows that asynchronous decoupling is what makes it usable.

findings.claim: Real-time-priority threads that initialise CUDA on CPU0 can hang CPU0 and crash the Orin kernel when sched_rt_runtime_us=-1; NVIDIA calls this 'a limitation rather than a bug' and says to run such work on other cores. Untuned PREEMPT_RT on AGX Orin shows cyclictest maxima of 1074-6221 us, and two identical AGX Orin 64 GB modules under the same isolated-core JetPack 6.2 RT setup differed 10 us vs 90+ us.

findings.relevance: Operational guardrails for Parcel's controller: never mix RT priority with CUDA init on CPU0, always isolate and tune, and validate each physical Orin module with cyclictest because silicon-to-silicon variance exists.

design_implications: Treat the Orin GPU as one time-sliced core: across processes there is no kernel concurrency, the quantum is ~1 ms, each context switch costs 50-750 us, and NVIDIA exposes no timeslice/priority knob on Jetson. Every extra GPU-active process adds wall time to the full-duplex speech model's 80 ms step roughly in proportion to that tenant's GPU time plus switch overhead.

Keep the 50-500 Hz body controller entirely off the GPU and on isolated CPU cores: RT OTA kernel + isolcpus=managed_irq,domain,8-11 irqaffinity=0-7 kthread_cpus=0-7 + mlockall gives ~15 us max jitter under GPU load on AGX Orin 64 GB, versus 159 us without isolation and 318 us on the stock kernel; never give a CUDA-initialising thread RT priority on CPU0; validate each physical module with cyclictest (10 us vs 90 us variance seen).

Collapse the GPU tenants (speech LLM, VLM, ASR, TTS) into one process using CUDA streams with priorities (non-preemptive hints, but enough when kernels are short), exactly as NVIDIA's Agent Studio does; only 4 usable compute channels per context on Orin caps intra-process parallelism. If a multi-process layout is unavoidable, use MPS (JetPack >= 6.1) with explicit active-thread percentages and benchmark it on the Orin first, since no Orin MPS measurement exists and dGPU reports show +10-40% per client and 100 ms stalls when misconfigured.

Do not plan on Thor-class isolation: green contexts, MPS-with-SM-isolation and MIG are Thor features; NVIDIA states Orin (sm_87) stays on its current path. Spatial partitioning on Orin is limited to intra-process green contexts with no concurrency guarantee or the research libsmctrl.

Memory bandwidth (204.8 GB/s shared by GPU, DLA, CPU) is the real bottleneck, not the 64 GB; single-stream LLM decode is bandwidth-bound, so every co-tenant steals decode tokens/s from the speech model. Offload detectors/trackers to the two DLAs where possible; keep VLM/ASR bursty and admitted opportunistically (LiteVLA-H's fast-act/slow-semantic K=3 pattern) rather than continuously.

Design the act-token path around asynchrony: single-tenant VLA-class heads cost 150-440 ms per step on Orin, and asynchronous inference (Jetson-PI) is what turns 0.7 Hz into 6 Hz; the body controller should hold/interpolate across late act tokens instead of blocking, and the 'look back when lost' / 'chuckle' behaviours should tolerate 100-200 ms act latency.

The decisive number for the one-clock speech+act design on a single AGX Orin does not exist in the literature: run a two-day microbenchmark on the dev Orin (cyclictest on isolated cores + a 1 kHz CUDA heartbeat-kernel logger while the candidate speech model decodes, then add VLM and ASR one at a time, recording per-step p50/p99) and make it a gate before committing to co-tenancy on one Orin versus splitting speech (external AGX Orin) from locomotion/perception (the dog's Orin NX).

Process-count hygiene: the 32-context ceiling is far for five models but reachable by a ROS 2 / Isaac ROS graph where many nodes open CUDA; set CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS deliberately and keep GPU-using nodes few.
